The 21-year-old forward arrived on Tyneside from Lille on deadline day and has featured as a substitute in Newcastle’s last two matches. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Manchester City travel to Old Trafford on Sunday seeking to continue their perfect start to life under Enzo Maresca and further prove Anderson’s point. The 23-year-old midfielder made his claim upon signing from Nottingham Forest for £116m in the summer and having from afar witnessed City win eight Premier League titles during the past 14 years, compared with United’s one.e

“I think Manchester City was unbelievable what they achieved. It’s normal when Elliot said that,” said Maresca. “If you go back it’s a different picture, but for me the reason he said that is because when he grew up Manchester City was dominant.”

Brazilian winger Kevin, an unused substitute against Crystal Palace, added a cryptic message on his Instagram story with the caption ‘no speak, no hear, no see’. Alex Iwobi and Emile Smith Rowe have, meanwhile, both cleared their own Instagram posts of football-related content, with some fans interpreting it as growing signs of disharmony within the Fulham camp.

Alvaro Arbeloa moved to calm waters today: ““You can learn more about a group after a defeat than after a win, and I saw them work during the week with a very positive attitude, all of them,” the Fulham boss said at a press conference.

“For sure when you are a player and you are not playing, you can’t be happy. It is what I expect from the players that are not playing. I want that they should need to show me that they are not happy during the training session. For me, this is the most important thing.

“Obviously, when you are not winning games and you are not helping your team, I think you have more desire to play games and to help their team-mates. But all of them, they have been working so hard and I have a very, very good group with a very good attitude.”

Time for another handover. John Brewin will be your news conduit for the next wee while. Catch you’se later.

Hull fined over offensive chanting. Anecdotally, you do detect a slight uptick in unpleasant chants from the tiresome edgelord element among clubs’ fanbases and Hull have copped a fine for the homophobic antics of some herberts in their support after last season’s Cup tie against Chelsea, as Reuters reports:

Hull City have been fined £30,000 ($40,512) by the Football ⁠Association over discriminatory chanting during their FA Cup defeat by ⁠Chelsea in ⁠February, ​the governing body said on Friday.

An independent regulatory commission also ⁠imposed an action plan on the club after it failed to prevent ⁠offensive chanting despite warnings over the public ​address system.

“It was ‌alleged that ‌the club failed to ensure its spectators ‌and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters) do not use words or behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, indecent or insulting way with a reference – whether ‌express or implied – to sexual orientation,” read the statement.

Offensive chanting was heard ​in sections of the home crowd during the first half of last season’s game, prompting an announcement over the PA ⁠system urging supporters to stop and reminding ​them ​that CCTV was in ​operation.

A second announcement was made ​in the ‌second half ​confirming ​action had been taken, including arrests made. Hull City have admitted the charges.

Some mid-morning reading: a lovely Moving the Goalposts piece by Tom Garry with Gemma Darvill, coach of the first England women’s Parkinson’s team and how restorative football has been for her dad, who lives with the condition.

When Gemma Darvill’s dad, Les, was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease aged 58, joining a walking football team stopped him from confining himself to his own home, and she believes the game saved his life.

What she could never have foreseen was that, eight years later, she would find herself coaching the first England women’s Parkinson’s team , helping transform the lives of women with the disease from all across the country. She is set to embark on a journey to Toronto to help spread awareness of the ways in which walking football can help put the brakes on the progression of Parkinson’s symptoms.

A teacher at Swallowfield primary school in Woburn Sands, in Milton Keynes, Darvill’s interest in walking football was sparked by supporting her dad. She now coaches what is believed to be the first walking football team specifically dedicated to women with Parkinson’s, the Parkinson’s Pioneers , who train in Solihull and have seen a tenfold increase in their membership in just over three years. That led to her appointment as the coach of the first England women’s national side.

There’s a lot of noise about Manchester United’s 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel , and the volume was ramped up last night when he scored a hat-trick for the U19s in their 5-0 win against Sabah in the Uefa Youth League. Gabriel has already trained with Michael Carrick’s first team and his coach Adam Lawrence sung his praises again after Thursday’s showing, reports PA.

“JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through,” Lawrence said. “He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.

“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into, so it’s good to see him enjoying his football in a good place.”

“The first thing is that it’s my job is not to ruin him. When you have a talented player like JJ and the other lads, you obviously don’t want to stifle their freedom and their creativity.

“What you try and do is to set the team up to allow the talent to function and to play free at the right moments. It can’t always be free and off the cuff, in terms of the off-the-ball responsibilities that he’s working on and the pressing that he’s thinking about.

“But in terms of how he plays properly and how he connects with other team-mates at the top end of the pitch, he’s just in a real good space.”

Nico O’Reilly is set to return to the Manchester City side for Sunday’s derby at Manchester United. The England left-back has missed the last two games after pulling up with a back problem in the warm-up prior to last weekend’s Premier League victory over Coventry.

Winger Jeremy Doku remains on the sidelines with the calf problem he sustained in the Community Shield but City have no other fitness concerns for the trip to Old Trafford. The manager, Enzo Maresca, said: “Nico is 100 per cent available but Jeremy, I think he needs some more days.” PA

Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.

Arsenal’s flight to Italy for their Champions League opener against Napoli this week was delayed for more than five hours , with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time. The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner .

Arteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previously employed pickpockets during pre-season training camps and preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker. The Arsenal manager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else. Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.

“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘Okay, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”

Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”

Morning everyone . Off to a game this weekend? What are your hopes and expectations? I always aim low in the vague hope of being pleasantly surprised.

The EFL’s monthly trinkets are in too, with Southampton’s Cyle Larin named Championship player of the month, while Jamal Lowe of Sheffield Wednesday and York’s Harry Boyes taking the League One and League Two awards respectively.

The manager awards in the EFL went to Vítor Matos of Swansea (Championship), Huddersfield’s Martin Drury (League One) and Dean Brennan of Barnet (League Two).

Thanks Tom . Hull City have confirmed that their winger Sorba Thomas was unhurt following a car accident this morning. After dramatic images were posted on social media, Hull issued a statement saying the Wales winger walked away unscathed.

Hull City is relieved to confirm that Sorba Thomas is unharmed following a road traffic accident near to the club’s Cottingham training ground.

The club is aware of images of Sorba’s car circulating on social media and can reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed.

I’m grabbing a break from the blog, to see you through the next couple of hours is Tom Davies.

Matthias Jaissle revealed that summer signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo is edging closer to starting for Newcastle .

The 21-year-old forward arrived on Tyneside from Lille on deadline day and has featured as a substitute in Newcastle’s last two matches.

Speaking ahead of Monday’s clash with Leeds, Jaissle said: “Yeah, he’s getting closer. I said that we need to be smart with his load management. Now he’s getting more and more minutes.

“He has now almost a full training week to Leeds, that helps him a lot. I think it’s the first time now since he arrived, and then we can make the decision on Sunday, maybe even on Monday.” Press Association

Nicolas Jackson is ready to impress, Spurs are scrambled and the 199th Manchester derby takes place at Old Trafford.. here are our 10 things for the upcoming weekend of football:

Spanish World Cup-winner Juan Mata has confirmed he will be departing Australian side Melbourne Victory, but stopped short of calling time on his career.

The former Manchester United and Chelsea ace has enjoyed a late-career resurgence and was voted the domestic A-League player of the year in 2025-26.

But the 38-year-old has decided not to play on at the club as he mulls “the next steps in his career”.

He will remain involved with the Australian side after taking an ownership stake.

“I loved every minute and so greatly enjoyed everything that we achieved last season, falling back in love with football at such a special place, in an amazing city that it was a privilege to call home,” Mata said.

“Now I am excited about our next chapters, believing together in the future of Australian football and inspiring the next generation of Melbourne Victory players and supporters.” AFP

Gianni Infantino has not responded to a request to appear before the US House judiciary committee or sent documents requested by one of its members more than a month past the deadline.

The Democrat Jamie Raskin, the ranking minority member of the committee, wrote to the Fifa president on 26 July informing the Swiss he was launching an investigation into “a sustained campaign” by Fifa to curry favour with the US president, Donald Trump.

His letter said seeking of favours extended to the dismissal of high-profile corruption cases, while also accusing Fifa of “gouging” American consumers with “exorbitant” World Cup ticket prices this summer.

The Swiss was asked to respond to the letter by 9 August with the requested documents and to make contact with the committee to schedule an interview, but it is understood no response at all had been received as of Thursday.

Because no subpoena was issued, there are no criminal consequences for ignoring Raskin’s request. Press Association

In totally normal Turkish football news… the Fenerbahce head coach, Ismail Kartal, announced his resignation on Thursday after ⁠his team drew 1-1 at home to Roma in the Champions League – but minutes ⁠later, the club ⁠president ​said Kartal would stay in the job.

Kartal shocked the post-match press conference by claiming he was ⁠leaving Fenerbahce “never to return”. The 65-year-old added that he was taking the drastic decision “to clear the way for the club” – but the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildrim, quickly moved to play down his manager’s remarks.

Minutes after ⁠the press conference, Yildirim told reporters that ​Kartal “continues in his role” with the Turkish side. “Some ‌fans threw a bottle ‌at the coach’s head this evening during the game. He ‌is upset about it,” the club president added.

The French football federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, said Gianni Infantino had “seriously damaged the image and the unity of football” as he announced the end of France’s support for the Fifa president’s re-election.

The FFF’s executive committee unanimously voted on Thursday to withdraw its backing, which had been formalised at the end of June. Diallo referred to “events during the World Cup” which had “flagrantly gone against the way we believe our sport should be run” and to Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan, which was revealed in July and scrapped after a widespread backlash.

United were the only Premier League club in Champions League action last night but Englishman Harry Kane scored for the eighth game in a row in the competition as Bayern Munich beat Bodø/Glimt 5-0 at the Allianz Arena. Starting their Champions League journey were Cesc Fabregas’s Como, who beat RB Leipzig 4-1 Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, while Lens scored twice in added time to reverse a 2-1 deficit and secure a 3-2 win. Our roundup of all of Thursday night’s European action is here .

Manchester United were back in Europe’s elite competition after a two-year hiatus and in need of something to soothe them after the trauma of their last-gasp coughing up of two points in last Sunday’s Premier League draw at Everton. And before the extremely serious business of the derby here against Manchester City on Sunday. They got it on the back of a first-half performance that burned slowly before catching fire.

Sabah were game. United were clinical. It was Matheus Cunha who broke the deadlock midway through the first half and the defining moments came at the end of the period when Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko sent United into half-time with a three-goal cushion. Lisandro Martínez added the fourth late on. It was a case of job done for Michael Carrick, no wobbles. Now for City.

Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall has signed a new long-term contract with the club.

Reports suggest the left-back, 22, has agreed a two-year extension to his original deal that would take his contract up to 2031.

Hall has been the subject of interest from Manchester United, among others, but has now committed his immediate future to Newcastle.

“It’s an absolute pleasure to play for this club and to represent the supporters,” he said. “I know how much it means to them.

“To be able to bring joy to their faces, it’s a big thing for me. I obviously have a family connection with the club, which is incredibly important to us all.

“One of the main reasons I play is to make my family proud, and I know how much it means to them to watch me playing for Newcastle United.”

No club embraces chaos quite like Chelsea. Stability has been absent at Stamford Bridge going back even as far as the Ken Bates era. The latest twist in west London has been foreseen for a while, with warring factions between the current ownership meaning a parting of ways was always likely but Mark Walter’s issues with US tax authorities have accelerated the timeline. Then, on Thursday evening, Matt Hughes and Jacob Steinberg came through with the report that Chelsea’s majority owners, Clearlake Capital, are closing in on an agreement to buy out co-owners Todd Boehly and Walter in a deal that would see the pair make a profit on their investment and value the club at around £5bn.

We’ll be across any further updates on that story, plus the reaction to last night’s European action and all the other news ahead of the weekend football. Plenty to get stuck into.

articles.content:
26th over: Pakistan 100-2 (Azan 43, Masood 50) Masood edges Atkinson through the gap for four, then takes a single to reach a proud, determined fifty from 81 balls. It also brings up Pakistan’s first century partnership of the series .

It’s almost 100 and out when a vicious lifter hits Azan on the glove and lands short of square leg.

“I think what we should be considering over the winter is who should be the next captain,” says Stephen Brown. “Joe Root presumably wants to win the Ashes as captain next year. His record in those series is the biggest blot on his career. But who comes next?

“The best captains have always been the ones who looked like they would be captain for a while before hand. Root was talked about a captain for years before he became it. Same for Cook, Strauss, Vaughan etc. The ones who didn’t look like captain before they became it, but were picked because they were the best player (Flintoff, Pietersen are the examples that spring to mind) were often a lot less successful. Which is perhaps a long way of saying, it shouldn’t be Brook. But who should it be?”

I’m not sure Vaughan was talked about beforehand – Marcus Trescothick was the vice-captain for a few years. Brook reminds me of Vaughan, a flamboyant strokemaker whose apparently effortless brilliance hides a sharp cricket brain.

I guess it depends on the timing, but right now I’d say the likeliest scenario is that Brook becomes Test captain some time in 2027-28 with Jacob Bethell taking the white-ball jobs.

25th over: Pakistan 95-2 (Azan 43, Masood 45) Saying which, Masood has been dropped by the sub Theo Wylie at backward point. It was a sharp but relatively straightforward chance when Masood edged a drive off Tongue. I think he was beaten for pace.

At the end of the over Root runs up to Wylie, puts his arm round him and has a quick chat. “I can think of some captains who might not have been so empathetic…” deadpans Mike Atherton to his co-commentator, Nasser Hussain.

24th over: Pakistan 90-2 (Azan 43, Masood 40) Gus Atkinson replaces Ollie Robinson. He’s been the ghost at the feast, with one wicket for 172 runs in the series, even though he hasn’t bowled badly. Masood takes two and then a single to move into the forties. Pakistan’s batters look as secure as at any stage in the series.

23rd over: Pakistan 87-2 (Azan 43, Masood 37) Lovvvvvvvely batting from Azan Awais, who clips and drives Tongue for back-to-back boundaries. He’s had a tough series, with four single-figure scores in six, but there’s plenty to like. For a 21-year-old he is very organised and composed, and his cover drive is a thing of beauty. Pakistan should invest in him as they try to build a more competitive Test team.

22nd over: Pakistan 77-2 (Azan 33, Masood 37) Azan scrambles to make his ground after taking a tight single to mid-on. The substitute Taz Ali’s throw missed the stumps, though I think Azan would have been home. Pakistan are pottering along quite comfortably.

Coventry City in the Premier League, Warwickshire CC challenging for the county championship, England’s Test team with threatening 80mph bowlers. I’m starting to worry my dream about taking my GCSEs as an adult was actually a premonition.

21st over: Pakistan 76-2 (Azan 32, Masood 37) Time for England’s bulldozer, Josh Tongue, who has replaced Jofra Archer. Joe Root moves Ben Duckett from third slip to leg slip; moments later, Masood edges through third slip at catchable height. The ball runs away for four, and Masood gets another boundary with a crisp flick through square leg.

“One can’t help but wonder whether Joe Root has an LBW problem or a captaincy issue,” writes John Coutts. “The last time he was captain his batting deteriorated badly and it looks to be happening again.

“As far as the keeper standing up for fast-medium pacers is concerned, it seems to me there are two options in facing the good/full length ball: either get forward and risk a stumping or don’t get far enough forward and risk LBW or being bowled. The chance of a stumping is the lesser of the risks, therefore get forward. Joe Root and do that effectively therefore he should.”

His batting deteriorated for a while, but he also had the best year of his career in 2021. I think it’s too early to say that it’s affecting his batting, even though it’s a legitimate concern.

20th over: Pakistan 67-2 (Azan 32, Masood 29) Robinson bowls to Masood for the first time this morning. He starts over the wicket with the keeper standing back; Masood defends a series of straight deliveries. Robinson’s figures are delicious: 10-6-12-2.

19th over: Pakistan 67-2 (Azan 32, Masood 29) The sun is out at Edgbaston, so there are runs to be made as the ball gets older and the bowlers wearier.

18th over: Pakistan 66-2 (Azan 32, Masood 28) Azan pulls Robinson crisply in front of square for two. Robinson reverts to a good length and goes past the edge with successive deliveries before having an LBW appeal turned down on height. Beautiful bowling.

17th over: Pakistan 64-2 (Azan 30, Masood 28) Masood pushes Archer pleasantly through mid-off for a couple. There’s a lot to like about him as a batter; it’s hard to reconcile the eye test with an average of 30 from 50 Tests.

Lunch is at 1.15pm today, with tea at 4.10pm. That’s to make up some of the time that was lost yesterday.

16th over: Pakistan 60-2 (Azan 29, Masood 25) Robinson stays around the wicket to Azan, who has to play more because of the angle. After a few defensive strokes, Azan misses an attempted pull at a ball that bounces down the leg side for four byes. Jordan Cox, standing up to the stumps, didn’t have much chance with that. As Ian Ward points out on Sky Sports, those byes will go against Jamie Smith’s name rather than Cox’s.

The over ends with a spiteful delivery that lifts from a length to hit Azan in the chest. Sheesh.

“I know this is heresy, but should we be worried about Joe Root?” writes Chris Goater. “I know his record is amazing, and he has solved technical problems before, but he is surely getting towards the end of his time now. How much patience should the selectors show, if his run of low scores continues?”

One word, two syllables: WOW. A pattern of dismissals is always a bit of a concern, but the keeper won’t be up to the stumps as regularly when England play South Africa and Australia.

15th over: Pakistan 56-2 (Azan 29, Masood 25) An eventful over from Archer to Masood: two plays and misses, a lovely drive for four and an inside-edged pull onto the body that lands short of Archer.

“A whole three-match played with the same XI; no injured bowlers, no messing around by the selectors,” says Stephen Nichols. “More of this please!”

14th over: Pakistan 52-2 (Azan 29, Masood 21) Ollie Robinson starts over the wicket to Azan Awais, who is beaten by his second, third and fifth deliveries. Robinson moves around the wicket for the final ball of an excellent maiden. His grandkids are going to hear a helluva lot about the summer of 2026.

“Wow, the royalties from Kaiser have really added up!” banters Matt Dony. “When you’re sunning yourself on your private island, enjoying your millions, I hope you remember all the little people who got you there. Maybe we can invoice you on a per-email basis?”

13th over: Pakistan 52-2 (Azan 29, Masood 21) Archer’s second ball of the last day is a seaming lifter that beats Shan Masood’s defensive grope.

Time for the action Jofra Archer, whose fourth over was rudely interrupted by the dustmen rain last night, will open the bowling.

We don’t usually start the day’s play by directing you towards the Guardian’s country diary, but this is well worth your time.

“I know you have spent a lot of time and money trying to get your overdue payment,” writes Pastor J B Norble. “I am very sorry for this trouble and the inconvenience it has caused you. We have reviewed your payment file, and your payment of [$30,800,000] is now actively processed.”

State-school cricket has had its day at Lord’s, at last. On a ground that has this summer hosted men’s and women’s international Tests, the Women’s T20 World Cup final and the Hundred finals, on Thursday four school teams played in front of the Pavilion and Father Time for the Knight-Stokes Cup, named after two state-educated cricketers who have captained England’s Test teams.

Heather Knight and Ben Stokes recorded video messages for pupils from Altrincham grammar school, John Hampden grammar school, Penistone grammar school and Chelmsford County high school before they competed in the boys’ and girls’ finals. The privileges did not stop there – full use of the Pavilion dressing rooms, lunch and media duties made this a day to remember and inspire.

It’s a big day in the race for the County Championship. The peerless Tanya Aldred is your guide.

A few hours after his yelp of frustration echoed around Edgbaston , an innings of 65 and the growing conviction that “I was going to make a really big score” ended when he chased a wide delivery and played on, Dan Lawrence’s emotions had settled into something approaching contentment. England had taken a firm grip on the game, Pakistan ending the second day still 268 away from making them bat again with eight wickets remaining, and Lawrence, having posted three half-centuries in four Test innings this summer, is finally delivering on his obvious potential in an England shirt.

“I’m obviously gutted I didn’t kick on,” he said. “I felt like I was playing really nicely and it was a really good surface to bat on against a tiring attack at that stage. I thought I was going to make a really big score, but it wasn’t meant to be. But I’m really happy with how I’ve played [this summer].

The lack of Ashes cricket in the north of England next summer is the result of a legal dispute that followed the allocation of venues for the 2023 series against Australia, which also involved the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) paying about £1m in damages to Hampshire .

The Guardian can reveal that Hampshire brought a legal challenge against the ECB after missing out on hosting the Ashes in 2023 to Yorkshire, who staged the third Test – which England won by three wickets – at Headingley.

Hampshire are understood to have challenged the 2023 allocation on the grounds the club said they were promised their first Ashes Test at the Rose Bowl that year at a meeting of the 18 first-class counties in 2018.

“Good morning Rob,” writes Krishnamoorthy V. “If only Pakistan had a VVS Laxman and Rahul Dravid in their midst...”

There was a Pakistan fan walking around Edgbaston carrying a small blackboard on the second day . “Free Imran Khan …” he’d written on it, “and get him in the team.” He stopped to talk about it with a couple of the police officers standing guard around the back of the pavilion. “I’d like to report a crime,” he told them, “by the 11 players out there on the field.” The officers chuckled. “Not much I can do about that for you, sorry.” Even their supporters seemed to have reached the point where they just want this tour to be over.

With dismal inevitability, the weather had turned by the time Pakistan actually got out to bat in their second innings and the bright sunshine that lit up England’s batting through the afternoon had been occluded by a bank of heavy grey cloud that had blown up from the south-west. They turned the floodlights on just in time for Saim Ayub and Azan Awais to go out and face up to another new-ball burst from Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer. The lights didn’t help anyone, if anything they only made it easier to see what was coming.

Pakistan are averaging 15.90 runs per wicket in this series. That’s the lowest against England, in a series of three matches or more, since New Zealand were spun into oblivion by Tony Lock and Jim Laker in 1958.

Weather watch The sun is out at Edgbaston and play should start on time. The forecast is pretty good all day, so England should have plenty of time to get the job done and begin their end-of-series celebrations. Lime cordials all round.

Friday is the only sold-out day of this third Test but whether that translates into a full house remains to be seen. Much like the series itself, the contest is long since over, set in motion by Pakistan’s howling collapse on the first day and then compounded by England’s ruthlessness on the second.

Although for all that England’s march to a 3-0 clean sweep appears a formality, there should in theory be a decent chunk of cricket to enjoy. Joe Root’s side are still eight wickets away from enjoying a weekend at leisure, with Pakistan, set to resume on 52 for two, 268 runs away from making them bat again.

It follows a dominant outing with the bat from England that turned 156 for four in the morning into 453 all out by tea. That said, three men still trudged off despondently. Harry Brook needlessly ran himself out on 75, Dan Lawrence chopped on for 65, while Jamie Smith fell for 69 after batting through the pain of a suspected broken finger. In all three cases, a Test century went begging.

It’s the last day of term, kids. Wear what you like, play a bit of Subbuteo, talk to the people you’re usually too shy to talk to. England will wrap up a crushing, slightly sad 3-0 win over Pakistan sometime this afternoon, and Ollie Robinson will smile modestly after collecting yet another award.

Robinson continued his Lohmannesque summer – 28 wickets at 7.75 apiece – by taking both Pakistan wickets to fall yesterday afternoon. Pakistan will resume on 52 for 2, still 268 runs behind. They’ve got two chances, Slim and none. And the selectors sent Slim home.

articles.title: Fremantle Dockers v Geelong Cats: AFL semi-final – live
articles.summary: Updates from the winner-takes-all clash at Optus Stadium Sign up for our AFL newsletter | Any thoughts? Send an email The national anthem and Welcome to Country are sung and done. Dockers captain Alex Pearce and Cats skipper Patrick Dangerfield have tossed the coin. Hells Bells is ringing out for the top of the grandstand at Optus Stadium. And it’s time to buckle up to see if Fremantle can rise to the occasion against Geelong … Sign up for our free weekly AFL newsletter – From the Pocket Nick Watson produced his usual bag of wizardry tricks and James Sicily led a rock-solid defence as Hawthorn ended Fremantle’s perfect home record in brutal fashion with a stunning 32-point qualifying final win in Perth. The Hawks kicked six goals to one in a dominant first half in Thursday night’s clash to set up the 10.12 (72) to 5.10 (40) win and secure a home preliminary final. Continue reading...

Josh Treacy takes the sting out of the occasion as he slices a set shot for a behind. The ball bounces between the arcs before the Cats finally get it deep into their forward 50. Dangerfield throws off a tackler to get a handball out to Cameron who snaps a goal from a near-impossible angle. This is shaping up as a classic final.

Hayden Young streams out of the centre ball-up and rushes forward with one bounce, up to the edge of the square and rockets the ball over the goalline. That’s a fifth goal from centre clearance to the Dockers, and the third in barely 10 minutes in the second term.

The Cats win a rare centre clearance as Edwards dishes the ball off to Holmes who bombs it long inside 50. Dangerfield spills a chest mark while sliding on the turf and the crumbs end up with Shaun Mannagh streaming past.

Jye Amiss too strong as he outmuscles Jack Henry in a one-on-one at the top of the goalsquare. Dead-eye Jye makes no mistake.

Back-to-back goals to the Cats for the first time this evening. Shannon Neale stands out the back of a scrambling contest inside 50. He receives a handball out of the pack, has time to take one step and snaps another critical goal.

Fremantle have found it easier to go end-to-end as they quickly switch the ball but now Geelong open them up with a couple of changes of lane. Dangerfield marks out wide, plays on and kicks long to Oliver Henry who sneaks the ball just on the inside of the goal post for a much-needed major.

The Dockers pick up where they left off in the first term and win the centre clearance. A squaring kick from deep in the forward pocket picks out Isaiah Dudley and the livewire extends the home side’s lead.

Mark Blicavs is in the ruck for the Cats as the second term is about to get under way …

Luke Jackson has had nine disposals, two clearances and 10 hit-outs as a key to the Dockers’ bright start, with Hayden Young (seven, two) also critical. Shai Bolton and Patrick Voss helped finish off the work with a couple of goals apiece, while the Dockers dominated with 12-7 clearances including 6-2 in the centre. Milestone man Bailey Smith (seven) played almost a lone hand for the Cats and Chris Scott is showing no signs of panic at the first break.

An emphatic response from Fremantle after they failed to fire a shot in the qualifying final against Hawthorn. The minor premiers lead the Cats by 25 points with their scintillating ball movement up and running again. But their advantage at stoppage has been just as crucial with Luke Jackson teaching young Mitch Edwards a lesson.

The Dockers win the centre clearance again but Hayden Young misses his kick and the ball trickles out for a throw-in just inside the arc.

The Cats are under pressure even as they move the ball into their forward 50. Mitch Edwards is within range but kicks to the top of the goalsquare where Oliver Wiltshire is in front and marks on the move to goal and claw his side a little closer.

Fremantle give Geelong no time or space as the Cats try to exit their half-back line. Murphy Reid’s misplaced kick inside 50 is cut off and the Cats are happy to slow the game down with finish line of quarter time now in sight.

Fremantle open up Geelong on the outside again and Mason Cox has enough space to mark unattended. The Dockers recruit slots the set shot and here comes his usual carry on, this time in the face of a bemused Jack Henry.

Geelong move the ball at will from a Fremantle behind but miss the last kick inside 50. Jeremy Cameron shows no signs of his arm issues as he wraps up Luke Jackson in a tackle but the Dockers switch the ball across the last line again to go end-to end. Patrick Voss pulls down the mark this time and nails the set shot from the 50m arc. The Dockers have five – as many as they kicked in the entire game against the Hawks.

Geelong are one of the best sides in the competition at winning the ball back in their own forward half. They lock the ball forward again before Fremantle switch the play and transition with ease. Voss sets up for a mark over the back but Jye Amiss comes across to spoil him.

Fremantle have learned the lessons from their qualifying final defeat to Hawthorn as they look to move the ball with speed rather than falling back into the slow and sideways movement of last week.

Shannon Neale has perhaps the most pleasant kicking action in the game. But Cats’ fans won’t have enjoyed watching that one as the key forward hooks a shot from within range.

Hayden Young takes a mark inside 50 but slices the set shot from just inside the arc. Young Geelong ruck Mitch Edwards would like his time again after failing to impact the contest as the only big man in the vicinity.

Fremantle open up Geelong on transition with Murphy Reid scrambling the ball forward and Shai Bolton launching another long bomb to get over the last line of defence. Zach Guthrie does well running back with the flight of the ball to prevent a Isaiah Dudley mark inside 50, but Michael Frederick picks up the crumbs and goals.

The finals heat is dialled up with intense pressure making the footy hot and kicks now missing targets. The Cats have the ball in their forward half but can’t get a sight on goal.

Danger signs early for Geelong. And just the moment for their skipper to step up. The Cats scramble the ball to their 50m arc just inside the boundary where Patrick Dangerfield receives a handpass from Shannon Neale, scoots a few steps away from the boundary and launches a bomb to continue the blistering start.

The Dockers win the ball out of the middle again but the Cats defence pick off Bolton’s kick inside 50. A quick transition from the Cats is turned around by their former defender Jordan Clark who sliced through the centre square and kicks over the last line of defenders to Patrick Voss. The firebrand forward barely had a touch last week. But he has an early goal and the Dockers are rocking.

Shai Bolton has two and the Dockers are flying. Luke Jackson wins the centre clearance again, this time with Bolton’s help in the middle. He gets on the end of the chain and slams home the Dockers’ second from outside the 50m arc. The Cats are two goals down and yet to have a possession.

Shai Bolton gets the Dockers on the board. And he is pumped! Caleb Serong is all class after the Dockers get the first inside 50 and their midfielder picks out the goalsneak for the opener. Just the start the Dockers needed.

Luke Jackson and Mitch Edwards fly into each other in the centre circle as the AFL semi-final gets under way at Optus Stadium. And the Dockers ruck hacks the ball forward.

The national anthem and Welcome to Country are sung and done. Dockers captain Alex Pearce and Cats skipper Patrick Dangerfield have tossed the coin. Hells Bells is ringing out for the top of the grandstand at Optus Stadium. And it’s time to buckle up to see if Fremantle can rise to the occasion against Geelong …

As though Fremantle and their fans need a reminder of how their grand plans fell apart last Thursday at Optus Stadium – but with the first ball-up just a few minutes away, quickly catch up on how we ended up back at the same venue this evening …

Nick Watson produced his usual bag of wizardry tricks and James Sicily led a rock-solid defence as Hawthorn ended Fremantle’s perfect home record in brutal fashion with a stunning 32-point qualifying final win in Perth. The Hawks kicked six goals to one in a dominant first half in Thursday night’s clash to set up the 10.12 (72) to 5.10 (40) win and secure a home preliminary final.

Jonathan Horn will be reporting on this Fremantle and Geelong semi-final after being at the MCG this time last week as the Cats knocked out the Blues.

When Carlton jumped out to a 21-point lead, they had the 10 leading possession winners on the ground. But the Cats finally got some cohesion and fluidity in their game, with their fleet of small-to-medium hybrid players – Gryan Miers and Brad Close in particular – finding space and using the ball well. As the rain teemed down and the legs got heavier, Geelong began to look like the superior side. And Patrick Dangerfield began to bend the elimination final to his will.

Dangerfield had been a crucial player when Carlton dominated early. His snap around his body in the first term – in the same part of the ground where he terrorised Hawthorn in the preliminary final last year – helped keep the Cats in the contest. But he was magnificent in the second half.

Fremantle are staring at a straight-sets exit as they host the experienced Geelong with a preliminary final against Sydney up for grabs. Here is where the game will be won – and lost …

The slow ball movement that held the Dockers back in recent years returned against the Hawks and made it difficult to capitalise on their 57 inside 50s as they finished with only five goals. After scoring only 17 points from turnover against the Hawks, Longmuir’s side will have to punish the Cats’ mistakes more to progress to the preliminary final.

The Cats have got the balance between defence and attack right across their unbeaten run home and into the elimination final win against the Blues, with six scores of 100 points or more in the seven victories while conceding triple figures only once.

Fremantle and Geelong fans are flocking to Optus Stadium with the first ball-up a bit over half an hour away.

Geelong midfielder Bailey Smith is playing his 150th AFL match . He played 103 of those for Western Bulldogs before moving to Geelong in the 2024 trade period. But he has lived up to the hype at his second club while averaging 31.9 disposals across 46 games and finishing third in last year’s Brownlow medal in his first campaign since recovering from a torn ACL.

The nerves will be jangling for Fremantle fans at Optus Stadium and far beyond with their dreams of claiming the club’s first men’s premiership back on shaky ground. Brendan Foster is in Perth and has seen the hype grow across this AFL season as well as the Dockers’ previous, all ultimately failed, finals campaigns.

Whenever the Dockers make a finals appearance, the ramshackle, salty seaside port city of Fremantle becomes awash in a sea of relentless optimism. The city’s famed Cappuccino Strip and nearby streets are painted purple; Dockers-themed sausages that eerily resemble the entrails of Frankenstein are on the menu at cafes and restaurants, and landmarks like the World Heritage-listed Fremantle prison light up with a peculiar, pale plum colour.

The only thing missing is Prince & The Revolution’s 1984 banger Purple Rain bellowing out of loudspeakers in the heart of the CBD.

Fremantle made one change from the side that was humbled by Hawthorn in the qualifying final with winger Nathan O’Driscoll dropped and defender Brandon Walker forced out with an ankle injury. The versatile Corey Wagner comes in to face Geelong with former Melbourne defender Judd McVee also recalled for the semi-final.

Geelong are unchanged from the team that overwhelmed Carlton last week after electing not to recall tall defender Sam De Koning even with Fremantle naming three key forwards in Josh Treacy , Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss .

Hello and welcome to live coverage of the AFL’s semi-final between Fremantle and Geelong . There is a strong sense that we have reached the pointy end of the season when the minor premiers and perennial finalists cross paths. But this meeting between the Dockers and the Cats might have come a week or two earlier than most would have predicted after a wild weekend of finals, or at least among the top-four sides of the home-and-away season.

The Dockers gave up much of the ground they gained when breaking a club record for their longest winning streak (now 14 matches) and most victories in a regular season campaign (now 19) with a disastrous qualifying final against the Hawks. Justin Longmuir’s side were already lined up to host two finals but the second now comes a week earlier than they would have hoped with a knockout game against Chris Scott’s finals-hardened side. The prize of a preliminary final berth is still there for the taking, though the ignominy of a straight-sets finals exit even after finishing on top of the ladder will only add to the pressure on the home side.

The Cats took time to get going against the in-form Blues in their elimination final. But once they clicked, the result soon felt like a formality and they pulled away to a comfortable 33-point victory that might have been much more if not for booting 23 behinds from 37 scoring shots. In a reminder of the finals experience that the Cats will bring, they have won 13 finals since 2015 while the Dockers have won only one.

Last year’s runners-up still have room for improvement with Max Holmes on the comeback trail from a serious ankle injury and Jeremy Cameron still looking underdone. The gun forward only gathered nine disposals as he played a combination of wing and defence last week, while he manages shoulder/AC joint problems as well as lingering nerve issues with the right arm he broke in last year’s grand final defeat to the Lions. But the Cats will hope both of the pivotal players are better for the run.

The winner of this semi-final will like their chances against the undermanned Sydney in a preliminary final at the SCG. But for now – first ball-up at Optus Stadium in Perth is 6.10pm local/8.10pm AEST . I’ll drop in team news shortly. Meanwhile, shoot me an email with your thoughts and predictions. Let’s get into it!

articles.content:
Enzo Maresca has backed Elliot Anderson’s assessment that Manchester City are the “ kings of Manchester ” as he prepares for his first derby in charge of the club.

City travel to Old Trafford on Sunday seeking to continue their perfect start to life under Maresca and further prove Anderson’s point. The 23-year-old midfielder made his claim upon signing from Nottingham Forest for £116m in the summer and having from afar witnessed City win eight Premier League titles during the past 14 years, compared with United’s one.

“I think Manchester City was unbelievable what they achieved. It’s normal when Elliot said that,” said Maresca. “If you go back it’s a different picture, but for me the reason he said that is because when he grew up Manchester City was dominant.”

Meanwhile, Michael Carrick suggested the short turnaround after United’s Champions League win over Sabah on Thursday night was “not ideal”, especially given City had a further two days to prepare for the fixture, having beaten Porto away on Tuesday . Pep Guardiola was often vocal on the subject of fixture scheduling but Maresca has taken it more in his stride and offered little sympathy to his opposite number. “To be honest, the club mentioned to me that it happened exactly the same last year when the club played Napoli and then after two days played Arsenal,” he said.

“Sometimes it happens in football. I don’t have any doubt that Man United are going to be ready for that. It just matters to adapt. I think that happens and you need to adapt. It happened last year with us, this season with them, next season it will happen with a different team.”

Maresca will welcome back Nico O’Reilly after the midfielder was a late withdrawal from the win over Coventry last week and missed the trip to Portugal with a back problem, but Jérémy Doku is not fit to return from a calf injury picked up in the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal .

Across his career as a player and coach, Maresca has been involved in some of the game’s biggest rivalries, enjoying the Manchester derby as part of Guardiola’s backroom staff. “I promise you the worst one is Olympiakos-Panathinaikos [in Athens]. That is very hot.” Maresca said. “I think they [derbies] are all special games for everyone. For the fans, first of all, for the club, for the players, for the coaching staff.”

Meanwhile, Michael Carrick suggested the short turnaround after United’s Champions League win over Sabah on Thursday night was “not ideal”, especially given City had a further two days to prepare for the fixture, having beaten Porto away on Tuesday . Pep Guardiola was often vocal on the subject of fixture scheduling but Maresca has taken it more in his stride and offered little sympathy to his opposite number. “To be honest, the club mentioned to me that it happened exactly the same last year when the club played Napoli and then after two days played Arsenal,” he said.

“Sometimes it happens in football. I don’t have any doubt that Man United are going to be ready for that. It just matters to adapt. I think that happens and you need to adapt. It happened last year with us, this season with them, next season it will happen with a different team.”

Maresca will welcome back Nico O’Reilly after the midfielder was a late withdrawal from the win over Coventry last week and missed the trip to Portugal with a back problem, but Jérémy Doku is not fit to return from a calf injury picked up in the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal .

Across his career as a player and coach, Maresca has been involved in some of the game’s biggest rivalries, enjoying the Manchester derby as part of Guardiola’s backroom staff. “I promise you the worst one is Olympiakos-Panathinaikos [in Athens]. That is very hot.” Maresca said. “I think they [derbies] are all special games for everyone. For the fans, first of all, for the club, for the players, for the coaching staff.”

articles.title: Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe v USA finely poised as day one fourballs begin – live
articles.summary: ⛳️ Solheim Cup updates from 6.40am BST at Bernardus Golf ⛳️ Live scores | And send any thoughts to David via via email Europe do indeed escape from their travails on 1 with a half. Alison Lee leaves her birdie putt short, and Nanna Koertz Madsen tidies up. But the USA strike back on 2, Nelly Korda wedging close with her approach on the par five, and Lottie Woad can’t save the day with her 15-foot right-to-left putt. All square in the opening two matches. Corpuz/Korda A/S Hull/Woad (2) Koerstz Madsen/Boutier A/S Coughlin/Al. Lee (1) Continue reading...
articles.content:
One notable conversation point after seeing the fourballs is that all 24 players will have had a hit on the opening day. That has to be good for team morale surely. Then again, will Leona Maguire be smiling through gritted teeth? Her record in this event is phenomenal, now reading 9-3-1 after this morning’s win. There was surely a strong argument to send her out again although the line-ups were likely decided some time in advance.

European skipper Anna Nordqvist waves enthusiastically to the crowds surrounding the first tee box. She even does a jig to some folk dressed as bananas. Well, why wouldn’t you? Support from fruit is always welcome.

Thanks Scott! Well, what a fascinating morning that was. The first opening session to be tied since 2015 at St. Leon Rot in Germany. That one finished 14.5-13.5 to the USA and it’s hard to see this year’s edition being anything but tight. Indeed, a number of shrewd judges have even gone for the tie – the outcome that unfolded at Finca Cortesin in Spain in 2023.

12.05pm (BST): Charley Hull and Lottie Woad v Yealimi Noh and Angel Yin 12.20pm: Celine Boutier and Nanna Madsen v Megan Khang and Alison Lee 12.35pm: Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud v Allisen Corpuz and Auston Kim 12.50pm: Carlota Ciganda and Julia Lopez Ramirez v Nelly Korda and Lauren Coughlin

Something of a surprise that Boutier and Madsen have been given another run-out, because neither player was anywhere near their best this morning. A good chance to right some wrongs, though. Penny for the thoughts of Leona Maguire, who it’s safe to say usually doesn’t care too much for being stood down.

Your friend and mine, David Tindall will take you through the afternoon action. Enjoy, enjoy, and I’ll see you all again tomorrow morning.

That was a fantastic morning of matchplay golf. Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda made Solheim Cup history by becoming the first pairing to post a five-and-zero record in foursomes. They were magnificent, but then so was Lottie Woad, who made several crucial putts to keep the score semi-respectable. Leona Maguire, Maja Stark and Linn Grant did their usual thing for Europe, too. This is lining up to be one hell of a weekend. Incidentally, the USA had the honour this morning, hence the ordering of the scores, but allow me to cock a snook to consistency and switch everything around as we go into the rest of the tournament. So sue me! *

Hull/Woad v Corpuz/Korda 4&3 Madsen/Boutier v Al. Lee/Coughlin 3&2 2UP Henseleit/Maguire v An. Lee/Duncan 3&2 Stark/Grant v Zhang/Kupcho Europe 2-2 USA

Lee sets her putt rolling serenely towards the hole. It’s surely going in … but somehow it drifts to the right on its final turn and misses by the width of a dimple. Team USA pick up Leona Maguire’s coin – she’s got two putts from as many feet – and Europe win the match 2UP. Esther Henseleit and Leona Maguire beat Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan 2UP

Henseleit sends a crisp wedge flying towards the flagstick. Too fierce? Not a bit of it! The ball grips and spins, before rolling out to three feet. That’s a wonderful shot under pressure, and now Andrea Lee has to make the par putt if the USA are to realistically snatch half a point. But if there’s anyone the USA would pick to take this putt, it’s surely Lee …

Lindy Duncan steps up to the plate. A wedge over the flag that lands 20 feet past before spinning back to ten. A chance for par. Over to Esther Henseleit, just off the front of the green …

Leona Maguire up first. She creams a hybrid and gives it a twirl, though the ball doesn’t reach the green, rolling to a halt a few yards short. Andrea Lee meanwhile hits a slightly heavy shot out of the bunker, the ball toying with the creek running across the middle of the fairway. But it gets over. The US pair are about 80 yards out, so an up and down for par is far from a pipe dream, and would put all sorts of pressure on the European duo.

… she sends her tee shot to the right again, just as she did on 16. But not so far that it goes into the bunker that (reportedly – the cameras haven’t shown it) snaffled Duncan’s ball. So it’s advantage Europe. Many hard yards to travel yet, though.

Lindy Duncan sends her tee shot into a bunker down the right of the 18th fairway. A world of possibilities opens up for Europe … but Esther Henseleit sent her last tee shot into the drink, so the nerves will be jangling. And …

Esther Henseleit rolls in the par saver! She fist-pumps the air and Europe are dormie. Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan will have to win 18 if the USA are to go into the afternoon fourballs with an advantage.

An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (17) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3&2 (F)

Europe’s ball on 17 is behind a hillock to the right of the green. Leona Maguire doesn’t have much room to work with, but she lands a graceful chip onto the far side of the bank, her ball rolling out to four feet. Andrea Lee’s long birdie putt stops just short of the hole, so Esther Henseleit will have the opportunity to make amends for her recent errors. But it’s no gimme …

… Rose Zhang holes her 15-foot right-to-left swinger! Europe have two putts for the win … and Maja Stark leaves a tentative dribbler a couple of feet short and wide left! Work to do … but Linn Grant completes the job. Europe on the board! Maja Stark and Linn Grant beat Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho 3&2

Europe might be denied in this last match, though. Esther Henseleit, a little shaken perhaps by the mistake on the 16th tee, sends her approach at 17 towards trouble to the right of the green. Lindy Duncan finds the putting surface in regulation. So this could be all square again soon. Then on 16 …

Linn Grant sends her wedge over the flag on 16, the ball spinning to a halt 15 feet past. Then it’s Jennifer Kupcho from the dropzone, which in a quirky twist is located further out than Grant’s ball. Kupcho gets a little bit closer than Grant, but only a gut-punching twist would deny Europe now.

Better news for Europe in the anchor match. Rose Zhang decides to go for the 16th green in two. She’s got little option but to roll the dice, because the USA are dormie three. And she doesn’t catch her fairway wood properly, sending the ball scampering apologetically into the creek guarding the front of the green. Maja Stark lays up in front of the water, and Europe are closing in on their first point of the week.

… and Europe’s quest for parity doesn’t begin well, as Team USA snatch a hole back in match three. Esther Henseleit’s errant drive proving costly in the end.

An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (16) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (15)

Europe still have an extremely good chance of salvaging parity from this morning session. But there’s plenty of work to be done to close out the last two matches, and if they somehow let things slip, it’ll be pretty dispiriting for the hosts.

3&2 Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (F) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (15)

… but she can’t do it. Madsen tugs a nervous effort wide left, never dropping, and it’s a 3&2 victory for the USA! Anything other than an American win would have been an affront, really, if we’re being totally honest with ourselves, because both Madsen and Boutier were way off their A-games. Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin beat Nanna Koertz Madsen and Celine Boutier 3&2

Celine Boutier leaves Europe’s long birdie putt on 16 four feet short. It had been bang on line, but she simply didn’t hit it. That gives Alison Lee the chance to win the match, which she nearly does, a big right-to-left swinger stopping a couple of inches short. So now Nanna Madsen has to make a missable putt to keep the match alive …

Jennifer Kupcho wedges to six feet from the dropzone at 15. But that still leaves Linn Grant with two putts for the win, and she cradles her effort to tap-in distance. The hole is conceded and Europe are dormie three in the anchor match.

2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (15)

More aquatic shenanigans. Esther Henseleit carves her drive at 16 into Boutier’s Creek. Hanging around for that ruling won’t have helped her there. Lindy Duncan dry. Meanwhile up the hole, Lauren Coughlin and Nanna Madsen find the green with their third shots. Neither particularly close. The USA will be much happier about that, given their 2UP advantage.

Back on the par-three 15th, yet another player dunks their tee shot into the lake to the left of the green! Rose Zhang the culprit this time. Maja Stark doesn’t make the mistake Celine Boutier did earlier, following up by aiming for the heart of the green. Safe and dry. Huge advantage to Europe, who can almost touch dormie three in the anchor match.

A big break for Europe. The referee decides the bridge is in Boutier’s road, so she’ll get relief. A drop, no closer to the pin, but still in the hazard. So she’s able to go from the right side of the bank to the left, closer to the fairway. And because any dropped ball would roll into the creek, she can place. She whips back into the fairway, and Europe are alive and kicking. Just.

Europe’s ball is dry. But it’s in the hazard. Boutier wants a line-of-sight ruling, with a spectator bridge ahead of her. However that’s not the route she’d be taking with her next shot, back onto the fairway, so the referee’s not having it. Not immediately, anyway. After some back and forth, it looks like Boutier will get her drop, but there’s going to be some more discussion. In the meantime, the putting contest on 15 is halved and the teams move on.

2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (14)

The rain continues to pelt down. As if it wasn’t wet enough, Nanna Madsen sends her tee shot dangerously close to the creek running down the right of 16. The camera loses the ball, so more on that when we have it. Meanwhile back on 15, both Leona Maguire and Andrea Lee find the depression in the middle of the green, short of the flag on the wrong level. And Maja Stark makes a missable six-footer on 14 for the half. Everything oscillating in the breeze at the moment, with all these matches on knife-edges.

2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (14) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (14)

Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan zig-zag their way up 14 like the Keystone Kops. They end up with double bogey, and should probably concede the hole, but allow Leona Maguire the opportunity to make her par putt and get the crowd going. And there are more roars on 15, where Alison Lee leaves her bogey putt short, opening the door again for Europe. Celine Boutier barrels through it by making the putt, and making up for her mistake from the tee. Europe still alive!

2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (14) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

To the drop zone! And onto the green from 100 yards. Nanna Madsen gets closer than Lauren Coughlin, the latter ending up at the bottom of a bowl in front of the pin, the former pin high on the correct shelf. There’s quite a bit of break on the USA putt, over a ridge, while the European chance is straighter and flatter. Big putting contest coming up!

It’s started raining quite heavily at Bernardus. Alison Lee takes some time to towel down her grip before taking her tee shot at the par-three 15th … then sends her ball into the drink! The door suddenly open for Europe … but then Celine Boutier follows her in! Boutier’s jaw nearly hits the floor. She went for the pin, bringing the water on the left into play, when the match situation demanded a safe route into the heart of the green. What a brain freeze. A huge chance to get back into the match spurned.

3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (14) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (13) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

Andrea Lee skelps a long-range birdie putt into the hole on 13. That almost slam-dunked into the cup, such was the speed it was travelling. Had it not hit the hole, the ball may have ended up in Belgium. Meanwhile on 14, Nanna Madsen makes up for her wild drive by nearly holing out from the heather to scramble a half. Dormie four avoided, but Europe are still on the brink.

4&3 Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (F) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (14) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (13) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

Charley Hull has to get aggressive with her putt on 15. She’s got to make birdie. Her effort sails miles past. Nelly Korda’s 20-footer lips out to a couple of feet. Lottie Woad has to make the par putt if she’s to have any chance of keeping Europe alive … and in it goes! She’s now rammed in four putts on this back nine! And yet it’s all been in vain. Allisen Corpuz tidies up for the half, and the USA win 4&3. Corpuz and Korda five-and-zero in this format! Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda beat Charley Hull and Lottie Woad 4&3

Lottie Woad and Allisen Corpuz both find the green at the par-three 15th. But Corpuz is closer, and so the first point of the day is within touching distance for Team USA now.

Nanna Madsen is put off by a rendition of the Viking Roar that soundtracked Norway’s World Cup campaign. Does a Dane need to hear that? Either way, she flays her drive at 14 into rubbish down the right. Europe have struggled badly in this second match, and dormie four looms.

4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (14) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (13) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (12)

Charley Hull makes the birdie putt, and Europe stay alive in the lead match! It ain’t over ‘til it’s over.

4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (14) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (13) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)

All is almost lost in the lead match, but Lottie Woad is not giving up without a fight. She responds to Allisen Corpuz coming up short of the green with her approach by sticking her second pin high to six feet. But Nelly Korda chips up to three feet, so Charley Hull will have to make the putt to extend. Meanwhile in match two, the USA go three up despite Alison Lee racing a birdie putt four feet past. Lauren Coughlin tidies up to take control of that one.

Andrea Lee does what Andrea Lee does so often. A 12-footer to save the half on 12. That’s a huge moment for the USA in match three, because Esther Henseleit had an opportunity to make birdie from similar distance just before.

5UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (13) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)

… but Korda isn’t missing from three feet. The USA go 5UP with five to play in the lead match. Europe teetering. And suddenly things are going in the wrong direction for the hosts in the anchor match, Jennifer Kupcho winning a putting contest with Linn Grant on 11 to win a second hole in a matter of minutes. Europe’s lead in that one sliced in half, quicksmart.

5UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (13) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (11) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)

Scrub that about dormie five? Lottie Woad makes another big putt, securing bogey and forcing Nelly Korda to make the USA’s par putt! That’s a third huge putt by Woad in four holes …

Nelly Korda sends her second into 13 over the back-right of the green. The door’s open for Europe … but Charley Hull follows Korda down there. Then after Allisen Corpuz bundles her chip up to three feet, Lottie Woad underhits her effort, the ball only just making the green before toppling back down the swale. Hull gives the putt up a good rap, but that flies ten feet past, and in a minute or so, the USA will be dormie five in the lead match.

Maja Stark can’t make a birdie putt on 10. Their opponents are on the par-five green in two, and close, so the hole’s conceded. Up on 11, Leona Maguire sends a dart at the flag, and Esther Henseleit tidies up for birdie and a two-hole advantage. And on 12, Nanna Madsen holes a tramliner from downtown to scramble a half. Alison Lee had sent her second very close, so that was some act of escapology.

4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (12) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (11) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (10)

Celine Boutier makes the awkward par putt on 11 to scramble a half. Even better for Europe: Maja Stark leaves Linn Grant in a bunker greenside at 9, only for Grant to hole out for par. Rose Zhang’s birdie putt suddenly looks a lot longer than it did, and dies away on the low side. Another half scrambled for Europe, and that’s one heck of a momentum-saver. But the inevitable happens on 12 after Lottie Woad’s visit to the water. Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda closing in on becoming the first pairing in Solheim Cup history to enjoy a five-and-zero winning record in this discipline.

4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (12) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (11) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (9) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 4UP (9)

Nanna Madsen gets super-aggressive with a putt from the fringe on 11. Her ball rolls 12 feet past. This match is getting away from Europe. See also the lead match, where Charley Hull sends Europe’s tee shot into the heather down the right of 12. Lottie Woad can’t get good contact on the ball, hitting it heavy and dunking it into a creek short of the green.

Lauren Coughlin walks in the eagle putt on 10 to double USA’s lead in match two. Esther Henseleit misses a short putt on 9 to gift a hole to the USA. And in the lead match, both teams get up and down from the side of the green, but once again it’s Lottie Woad grinding it out, rolling in a staunch six-footer to halve the hole. Without those two big putts on 10 and 11, Europe would be in a world of pain. Woad may be 3DOWN but she’s been mighty impressive on debut.

3UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (11) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (10) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (9) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 4UP (8)

Europe still have an extremely good chance of salvaging parity from this morning session. But there’s plenty of work to be done to close out the last two matches, and if they somehow let things slip, it’ll be pretty dispiriting for the hosts.
3&2 Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (F) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (15)

… but she can’t do it. Madsen tugs a nervous effort wide left, never dropping, and it’s a 3&2 victory for the USA! Anything other than an American win would have been an affront, really, if we’re being totally honest with ourselves, because both Madsen and Boutier were way off their A-games. Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin beat Nanna Koertz Madsen and Celine Boutier 3&2

Celine Boutier leaves Europe’s long birdie putt on 16 four feet short. It had been bang on line, but she simply didn’t hit it. That gives Alison Lee the chance to win the match, which she nearly does, a big right-to-left swinger stopping a couple of inches short. So now Nanna Madsen has to make a missable putt to keep the match alive …

Jennifer Kupcho wedges to six feet from the dropzone at 15. But that still leaves Linn Grant with two putts for the win, and she cradles her effort to tap-in distance. The hole is conceded and Europe are dormie three in the anchor match.
2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (15)

More aquatic shenanigans. Esther Henseleit carves her drive at 16 into Boutier’s Creek. Hanging around for that ruling won’t have helped her there. Lindy Duncan dry. Meanwhile up the hole, Lauren Coughlin and Nanna Madsen find the green with their third shots. Neither particularly close. The USA will be much happier about that, given their 2UP advantage.

Back on the par-three 15th, yet another player dunks their tee shot into the lake to the left of the green! Rose Zhang the culprit this time. Maja Stark doesn’t make the mistake Celine Boutier did earlier, following up by aiming for the heart of the green. Safe and dry. Huge advantage to Europe, who can almost touch dormie three in the anchor match.

A big break for Europe. The referee decides the bridge is in Boutier’s road, so she’ll get relief. A drop, no closer to the pin, but still in the hazard. So she’s able to go from the right side of the bank to the left, closer to the fairway. And because any dropped ball would roll into the creek, she can place. She whips back into the fairway, and Europe are alive and kicking. Just.

Europe’s ball is dry. But it’s in the hazard. Boutier wants a line-of-sight ruling, with a spectator bridge ahead of her. However that’s not the route she’d be taking with her next shot, back onto the fairway, so the referee’s not having it. Not immediately, anyway. After some back and forth, it looks like Boutier will get her drop, but there’s going to be some more discussion. In the meantime, the putting contest on 15 is halved and the teams move on.
2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (15) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (14)

The rain continues to pelt down. As if it wasn’t wet enough, Nanna Madsen sends her tee shot dangerously close to the creek running down the right of 16. The camera loses the ball, so more on that when we have it. Meanwhile back on 15, both Leona Maguire and Andrea Lee find the depression in the middle of the green, short of the flag on the wrong level. And Maja Stark makes a missable six-footer on 14 for the half. Everything oscillating in the breeze at the moment, with all these matches on knife-edges.
2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (14) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (14)

Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan zig-zag their way up 14 like the Keystone Kops. They end up with double bogey, and should probably concede the hole, but allow Leona Maguire the opportunity to make her par putt and get the crowd going. And there are more roars on 15, where Alison Lee leaves her bogey putt short, opening the door again for Europe. Celine Boutier barrels through it by making the putt, and making up for her mistake from the tee. Europe still alive!
2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (15) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (14) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

To the drop zone! And onto the green from 100 yards. Nanna Madsen gets closer than Lauren Coughlin, the latter ending up at the bottom of a bowl in front of the pin, the former pin high on the correct shelf. There’s quite a bit of break on the USA putt, over a ridge, while the European chance is straighter and flatter. Big putting contest coming up!

It’s started raining quite heavily at Bernardus. Alison Lee takes some time to towel down her grip before taking her tee shot at the par-three 15th … then sends her ball into the drink! The door suddenly open for Europe … but then Celine Boutier follows her in! Boutier’s jaw nearly hits the floor. She went for the pin, bringing the water on the left into play, when the match situation demanded a safe route into the heart of the green. What a brain freeze. A huge chance to get back into the match spurned.
3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (14) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (13) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

Andrea Lee skelps a long-range birdie putt into the hole on 13. That almost slam-dunked into the cup, such was the speed it was travelling. Had it not hit the hole, the ball may have ended up in Belgium. Meanwhile on 14, Nanna Madsen makes up for her wild drive by nearly holing out from the heather to scramble a half. Dormie four avoided, but Europe are still on the brink.
4&3 Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (F) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (14) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (13) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (13)

Charley Hull has to get aggressive with her putt on 15. She’s got to make birdie. Her effort sails miles past. Nelly Korda’s 20-footer lips out to a couple of feet. Lottie Woad has to make the par putt if she’s to have any chance of keeping Europe alive … and in it goes! She’s now rammed in four putts on this back nine! And yet it’s all been in vain. Allisen Corpuz tidies up for the half, and the USA win 4&3. Corpuz and Korda five-and-zero in this format! Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda beat Charley Hull and Lottie Woad 4&3
Lottie Woad and Allisen Corpuz both find the green at the par-three 15th. But Corpuz is closer, and so the first point of the day is within touching distance for Team USA now.

Nanna Madsen is put off by a rendition of the Viking Roar that soundtracked Norway’s World Cup campaign. Does a Dane need to hear that? Either way, she flays her drive at 14 into rubbish down the right. Europe have struggled badly in this second match, and dormie four looms.
4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (14) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (13) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (12)
Charley Hull makes the birdie putt, and Europe stay alive in the lead match! It ain’t over ‘til it’s over.
4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (14) 3UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (13) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)

All is almost lost in the lead match, but Lottie Woad is not giving up without a fight. She responds to Allisen Corpuz coming up short of the green with her approach by sticking her second pin high to six feet. But Nelly Korda chips up to three feet, so Charley Hull will have to make the putt to extend. Meanwhile in match two, the USA go three up despite Alison Lee racing a birdie putt four feet past. Lauren Coughlin tidies up to take control of that one.

Andrea Lee does what Andrea Lee does so often. A 12-footer to save the half on 12. That’s a huge moment for the USA in match three, because Esther Henseleit had an opportunity to make birdie from similar distance just before.
5UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (13) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (12) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)

… but Korda isn’t missing from three feet. The USA go 5UP with five to play in the lead match. Europe teetering. And suddenly things are going in the wrong direction for the hosts in the anchor match, Jennifer Kupcho winning a putting contest with Linn Grant on 11 to win a second hole in a matter of minutes. Europe’s lead in that one sliced in half, quicksmart.
5UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (13) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (11) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 2UP (11)
Scrub that about dormie five? Lottie Woad makes another big putt, securing bogey and forcing Nelly Korda to make the USA’s par putt! That’s a third huge putt by Woad in four holes …

Nelly Korda sends her second into 13 over the back-right of the green. The door’s open for Europe … but Charley Hull follows Korda down there. Then after Allisen Corpuz bundles her chip up to three feet, Lottie Woad underhits her effort, the ball only just making the green before toppling back down the swale. Hull gives the putt up a good rap, but that flies ten feet past, and in a minute or so, the USA will be dormie five in the lead match.

Maja Stark can’t make a birdie putt on 10. Their opponents are on the par-five green in two, and close, so the hole’s conceded. Up on 11, Leona Maguire sends a dart at the flag, and Esther Henseleit tidies up for birdie and a two-hole advantage. And on 12, Nanna Madsen holes a tramliner from downtown to scramble a half. Alison Lee had sent her second very close, so that was some act of escapology.
4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (12) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (12) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 2UP (11) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 3UP (10)

Celine Boutier makes the awkward par putt on 11 to scramble a half. Even better for Europe: Maja Stark leaves Linn Grant in a bunker greenside at 9, only for Grant to hole out for par. Rose Zhang’s birdie putt suddenly looks a lot longer than it did, and dies away on the low side. Another half scrambled for Europe, and that’s one heck of a momentum-saver. But the inevitable happens on 12 after Lottie Woad’s visit to the water. Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda closing in on becoming the first pairing in Solheim Cup history to enjoy a five-and-zero winning record in this discipline.
4UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (12) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (11) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (9) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 4UP (9)

Nanna Madsen gets super-aggressive with a putt from the fringe on 11. Her ball rolls 12 feet past. This match is getting away from Europe. See also the lead match, where Charley Hull sends Europe’s tee shot into the heather down the right of 12. Lottie Woad can’t get good contact on the ball, hitting it heavy and dunking it into a creek short of the green.

Lauren Coughlin walks in the eagle putt on 10 to double USA’s lead in match two. Esther Henseleit misses a short putt on 9 to gift a hole to the USA. And in the lead match, both teams get up and down from the side of the green, but once again it’s Lottie Woad grinding it out, rolling in a staunch six-footer to halve the hole. Without those two big putts on 10 and 11, Europe would be in a world of pain. Woad may be 3DOWN but she’s been mighty impressive on debut.
3UP Corpuz/Korda v Hull/Woad (11) 2UP Coughlin/Al. Lee v Koerstz Madsen/Boutier (10) An. Lee/Duncan v Henseleit/Maguire 1UP (9) Zhang/Kupcho v Stark/Grant 4UP (8)
