articles.title: Nottinghamshire face crunch day against Hampshire after rivals’ wins: county cricket, day four – live
articles.summary: Latest updates from around the county grounds Mail Tanya or comment BTL | Sign up for The Spin Rocky Flintoff smacks Langridge with gumption, just like dad would have done, for four, but the next ball is collected by long off and that is that. The gap between the two bottom teams shrinks to 18. Five wickets for the impressive JT Langridge in his second first-class match. Three for the very useful Kishore. A cracking 65 for young Rocky Flintoff. And that’s that, done and dusted in 31 minutes. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Currie (39) and Lumsden (13) have reduced the Hampshire chase to 69 which is not beyond the realms of possibility with a fair wind and a bit of luck.

Ashes to ashes – the reason why there is no Ashes Test in the north next year.

What a season he’s having – 57 wickets and counting, behind only Matthew Potts in Division Two. He is currently holding five for 24, having whistled out all of Kent’s top five. Kent 54 for five.

“I thought his ball to Hurst was one of the best I’ve seen all season. I think he’s just a natural wicket-taker. He’s got good assets.

“He’s tall, he swings the ball as well. So I think that makes him a huge threat with the new ball. And he’s got wicket-taking deliveries that will get very good batters out which is a really good trick to have. We’ll try to hang onto him but I’m not sure Somerset are going to allow us to have him for too long, sadly.”

I briefly forgot about Notts, who have almost tidied Hampshire up already. Olly Stone, bowling like a chestnut thoroughbred on a morning canter, has three including a brilliant catch by Mitch Hay. Watch and wonder here .

And now Middlesex slip and slide, four down, Max Holden scooped up at slip by long-legged Ben. Middx 103-4.

Meanwhile, at Derby, Kent are falling foul of an on-song Ben Aitchison, Kent 28-4.

A-whooping and a-hollering from the Glos dressing room, that’s two wins on the bounce after they turned over Derbyshire last week. Well played, it’s hard to turn that ship around.

Rocky Flintoff smacks Langridge with gumption, just like dad would have done, for four, but the next ball is collected by long off and that is that. The gap between the two bottom teams shrinks to 18.

Five wickets for the impressive JT Langridge in his second first-class match. Three for the very useful Kishore. A cracking 65 for young Rocky Flintoff. And that’s that, done and dusted in 31 minutes.

No seasons-end delights for Crawley, who gets an outside edge from Aitchinson for four. And now Compton in Aitchinson’s next over. Kent 12-2.

And tumbleweed starts to move about OT as a ninth wicket falls. This time Kishore, as Stanley props forward and dabs the ball in the air for Dhariwal at silly mid off. A weary Anderson strolls out and bumps gloves with young Flintoff.

A fourth wicket for the endearing Langridg e who is doing his prospects no harm at all in this match, pinning Noman’s pad to stump. Lancs 137-8.

The scoreboard waits for Noman , who sweeps Kishore for six into a sad-looking reduced party stand.

Noman Ali gets in t he way of a bouncer from Langridge and we pause for a helmet change. Meanwhile there are wickets at Hove (Thomas gone for 44) and from the first ball of the day at Chester le Street where Nathan Fernandes is undone by Kasey Aldridge.

There is rain in the Manchester air but unfortunately for Lancashire not enough to keep them off the pitch. Balderson falls third ball of the day to that man Langridge. Lancs 122-7

A heart-warming read and lovely pics from Billy Munday and Tom Jenkins at yesterday’s Knight-Stokes Cup.

In a round of staggering collapses, batting sides continued to strap on their roller skates and head to the ice rink. At Grace Road, Leicestershire were rumbled for 145, a 377 run-victory that puts Somerset back on the top of the table, that longed-for first title still in reach.

Somerset set Leicestershire 523 to win after waiting for New Zealand signing Henry Nicholls to reach his first Championship century. Craig Overton (four for 33) and Jack Leach (three for 30) then stormed through Leicestershire’s defences. The most entertaining moment for a loyal crowd was when a runaway husky frolicked on the pitch.

At Trent Bridge, defending champions Nottinghamshire were bowled out for 104 by a rampant Hampshire attack. Seventeen-year-old Manny Lumsden, bowling with fire and bounce, sprung out five for 36, including top scorer Joe Clarke for 37. Hampshire, set 178, were soon batting on a see-saw of their own against Olly Stone (three for 15) and Dillon Pennington (three for 18). They had stumbled to 61 for six when bad light brought temporary respite.

At Headingley, Essex fell foul of Kuldeep Yadav, whose six for 50 has almost ensured Yorkshire ’s Division One spot next season. At one stage Essex were 26 for five following on, but Paul Walter’s 48 and George Bell’s 28 ensured they passed 100. Kuldeep can tuck career-best match figures of 10 for 120 into his wallet. Sam Cook, who arrived late, unwanted at the Test, didn’t bowl a ball.

Northamptonshire took 20 points from their six-wicket victory over Worcestershire , leapfrogging promotion challengers Kent . They had a more difficult day at the County Ground against Derbyshire , who have set the visitors 434 to win after half centuries for Brooke Guest, Luis Reece and the in-form Martin Andersson.

Elsewhere, an unbeaten maiden first-class 50 from Rocky Flintoff gave Lancashire a glimmer of hope for their first win since April. They trail Gloucestershire by 128 runs with four wickets remaining.

Grace Road :Somerset 363 and 316-5dec BEAT Leicestershire 157 and 145 by 377 runs

Trent Bridge: Notts 377 and 104 v Hampshire 304 and 61-6 Hants need 117 to win

Derby: Derbyshire 300 and 352-8 v Kent 219 and 3-0 Kent need 431 to win

Chester le Street: Durham 252 and 374 v Middlesex 203 and 55-2 Middx need 369 to win

Old Trafford: Lancashire 134 and 120-6 v Gloucestershire 212 and 169 Lancs need 128 to win

New Road: Northamptonshire 289 and 96-4 BEAT Worcestershire 200 and 182 by seven wickets.

Good morning! The rain is not going to save Gloucestershire or Lancashire today, so tune in for a cascade of wickets/tight run chase here at Old Trafford. Elsewhere, Notts have Hampshire where they want them, as do Durham over Middlesex. Kent somehow need to see out the day against Derbyshire after promotion rivals Northants knocked over Worcestershire. And there’s gentle meandering to coo over at Hove. Play starts at 10.30am, do join us.

articles.title: Alstom to build new battery-electric train fleet
articles.summary: The government says the work will support thousands of jobs across the UK.
articles.content:
The new battery-electric TransPennine Express trains are set to enter service in 2034

Work to create the UK's first battery-electric trains for long-distance main line services is set to begin in 2028, the Department for Transport (DfT) has announced.

The 29 new Adessia Stream trains are expected to enter service in 2034 and will be built at Alstom's Litchurch Lane factory in Derby.

The government said the investment of almost £1bn would help support more than 350 jobs at Alstom and a further 6,000 jobs across the UK supply chain.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the new trains would deliver "faster, more reliable journeys to the north and thousands of British jobs for the next generation".

The managing director UK at Alstom said the fleet would transform journeys across northern England

He added: "I've lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came.

"And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments, and missed opportunities. Today, that starts to change."

The DfT said the trains would help deliver the TransPennine Route Upgrade's aim to boost capacity by 30%, with thousands of additional seats a day across the Pennines by the early to mid-2030s.

They will run between key destinations across the north including Liverpool Lime Street and Scarborough, Manchester Airport and Saltburn, and Manchester Piccadilly and Hull.

On sections of the railway that are not electrified, where trains currently use diesel engines, the new electric models would be able to run without emissions, the government said.

The DfT added journey times would be cut by up to 10 minutes between Manchester and Leeds, and up to 14 minutes between Manchester and York.

The trains will be bought by rolling stock company Rock Rail and leased to TransPennine Express, the government added.

Alstom, which boasts the largest rolling stock train manufacturing site outside of China, secured a £370m contract in 2024 to produce 10 new London Elizabeth line trains.

This came less than three months after a redundancy consultation put 1,300 jobs at risk at its Litchurch Lane factory, which dates back to 1876.

Rob Whyte, managing director UK at Alstom, called the latest agreement a "landmark moment for Britain's railway".

He said: "We're absolutely delighted. It's fantastic news for Alstom as a company but also for the city of Derby and the East Midlands.

"We have a period where new builds will stop until the TransPennine order starts, but we've already taken on some refurbishment works for CrossCountry and for ScotRail and we'll look to transfer as many people as we can into that area."

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander spoke to the BBC at Alstom, next to one of the new Elizabeth line trains.

She said: "It's fantastic news that a city like Derby, that's got such a proud railway heritage, is also going to be manufacturing that new fleet of trains for the north of England as well.

"It is good news. It's about building the railway that the country needs to support the economy, but it's also about making sure that, in our economic heartlands - places like Derby - we've got really high skilled jobs for the future.

"This contract alone means 40 extra apprentices here. It secures 350 jobs at this facility and will support over 5,000 jobs in the wider supply chain as well."

In a statement, DfT said journeys on the new fleet would be "quieter, smoother and more reliable", while offering "improved accessibility, more luggage space and onboard wi-fi".

Step-free boarding - the "elimination of gaps between the train and platform" - are also being promised as part of a commitment to accessibility, alongside three dedicated wheelchair spaces, two accessible toilets, family-friendly areas and cycle and buggy storage on each train.

articles.content:
A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types

W hen Charlotte Mensah was a young child growing up in Accra, Ghana in the 1970s, she would spend hours watching her aunties having their hair intricately threaded, an ancient African technique where hair is wrapped tightly using yarn or thread. She didn’t know then that she would go on to become one of the most influential hairdressers in the UK. Renowned for championing natural black hair textures in mainstream culture, she has worked as hairstylist to singers Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu, and the writer Zadie Smith.

According to Smith, in an essay she penned about Mensah’s magic earlier this year: “Charlotte can make a great mane of braids appear where previously there were only split ends and hair loss.”

A three-time winner of afro hairdresser of the year and the first black woman to be inducted into the British Hairdressing Awards Hall of Fame in 2018: the extraordinary course of her 40-year-long career is now the subject of an exhibition, Charlotte Mensah: Community Matters in west London. It charts her rise from growing up in the Ghanaian capital, through her early days as a junior hairdresser in London’s West End in the 80s, to styling celebrities for magazine covers.

The dynamics of black hair and the beauty industry have changed dramatically in this time. According to Madeleine Haddon, senior curator of the V&A East, who has worked with Mensah on the exhibition: “This is a story of Black British creativity and many of the prejudices and hurdles that she [Charlotte] had to overcome in the 80s and 90s, but also how she changed the beauty industry and transformed perceptions of black beauty.”

When Mensah moved from Ghana to Stonebridge, north-west London, aged 11, she first became conscious of her hair – and was bullied for it. Whereas the black children at her school wore their hair relaxed, in braids or in cornrows, Mensah had what she calls a “TWA” – a tiny weeny afro. “I turned up with this short hair and they all started laughing at me,” she says. “I used to cry … they just thought my hair was so funny and I looked like an alien.”

When she left school at 16 in the mid 80s, Mensah landed an apprenticeship at the first luxury black hair salon in the UK, Splinters in Mayfair, which opened in 1970. At that time, Mensah had only practised at home, styling her younger sister’s hair in “simple little braids, twists, cornrows”.

Splinters was worlds away from her bedroom in north London. The teenage Mensah was sweeping the floors at a salon where clients such as Diana Ross, and Flori Roberts – the eponymous owner of the first cosmetics brand developed specifically for women of colour – passed through the door. She then worked her way up through some of London’s top black hair salons, such as Terry Jacques in Knightsbridge, which was frequented by Luther Vandross and Brandy. “It opened my eyes to a bigger world that I didn’t think existed,” she says. “I saw those women that came into the salon, they were very independent, they had their own businesses, and I thought, ‘I want to be like one of these women’.”

In 1999, at the age of 29, Mensah opened her first salon, Hair Lounge in Kilburn. The location later moved to Portobello Road, in London’s Notting Hill, where, 25 years and countless awards later, Mensah can still be found braiding hair and chatting to customers every day. As Smith has written: “ Charlotte Tilbury is unlikely to do your makeup at the Selfridges counter, but Charlotte Mensah will definitely braid your hair in Ladbroke Grove. She’ll also weave it, cut it, blow it out, colour it, treat it, whatever you need. Her craft is her passion, and she applies it to everyone equally, from the pop star prepping for a show to the auntie getting ready for church.”

For the last 10 years, Mensah has also had an eponymous product line, a high-end range of hair oils and finishing mists. It grew out of a need – growing up in the 70s and 80s, relaxed hair and curly perms were the fashion, but the products necessary for them weren’t sold in mainstream shops. Mensah had to travel out-of-borough to buy brands such as Dax and Sofnfree, that were imported from the US.

Now the landscape has changed. Boots and Superdrug have designated afro hair sections stocked with brands such as Camille Rose and SheaMoisture, for different black hair types. The celebrity-owned beauty business wave has ushered in brands such as Pattern by Tracee Ellis Ross, Cecred by Beyoncé and UK-based afro hair care lines, such as Afrocenchix. “There’s more access,” says Mensah. “So if I’m a young black girl living in Sheffield, I can go into my local high street or online and find something for my hair, which never used to happen.”

Mensah has also pushed the creative potential of black hair styling into the mainstream. One of the pictures in the exhibition is a photograph of the British boxer Nicola Adams in a Grace Jones-style boxed afro on the cover of Vanity Fair UK, styled by Mensah. Others of her covers include model Jourdan Dunn with spiralling braids for Heroine magazine, the singer Celeste with cornrows on Found And Vision, and writer-actor Michaela Coel bare-faced with Bantu knots for New York Magazine.

Her aim now is to address the remaining social prejudices surrounding black hair types, the notion that natural, kinkier hair textures need to be “tamed” or straightened to look “beautiful”. In particular, the lack of access to hairdressers outside big cities trained to style black hair types is a significant barrier.

Last year, the BBC reported that out of 259 colleges in England, only 82 said they taught a curriculum inclusive of afro hair care, and women are still travelling across the UK to get their afro hair cared for. Mensah suggests that education on treatment and styling of different hair textures outside the European standard is needed to tackle the issue. She has set up her own academy, based in London and Accra, which offers a training and mentorship programme for hair stylists.

“You should be able to walk into any hair salon on your high street and have your hair done, [an experience] which doesn’t exist,” she says, referring to the fact that many stylists still do not have the expertise to work with hair of all textures. “That comes from the education system … I can do all hair types. So everyone else should be able to.”

articles.title: ‘Delay the meals’: Mikel Arteta reveals latest maverick Arsenal methods
articles.summary: Manager wants players to cope with things going wrong Other tactics include making dressing room even hotter Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality. Arsenal’s flight to Italy for their Champions League opener against Napoli this week was delayed for more than five hours , with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time. The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner . Continue reading...
articles.content:
Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.

Arsenal’s flight to Italy for their Champions League opener against Napoli this week was delayed for more than five hours , with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time. The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner .

Arteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previously employed pickpockets during pre-season training camps and preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker. The Arsenal manager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else. Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.

“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘OK, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”

Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”

Arsenal travel to Sunderland on Saturday night looking to extend their 100% start to the new campaign after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last year. Leandro Trossard scored Arsenal’s second goal before Brian Brobbey’s late equaliser and Arteta contrasted the Belgium forward’s reaction to leaving in the summer with that of Gabriel Jesus. “No one told me nothing,” said the Brazilian, who was made to train separately from the rest of Arsenal’s squad before moving to Barcelona. Trossard, meanwhile, was at the Emirates for last week’s win over Chelsea having joined Beskitas in July.

“Very surprised, to be fair, especially because with Gabriel I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” said Arteta. “And the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don’t know. It’s OK. Sometimes I understand when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don’t expect. Those things are reactive. Somebody has to be the bad cop; if I have to be, I have to be.

“What is important is normally what happens three months later, six months later. When Trossard comes in, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relation you have with all the players that they left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that’s the same case.”

articles.content:
EastEnders hides in a Guardian crossword and Guardian crosswords hide in a thriller

O ne way to ensure a novel gets my attention is a foreword that mentions crosswords, specifically the Guardian’s. I admit that this does not happen often, but it has just happened. Tony White’s Phantom at the Feast opens with this claim:

Words emboldened in the text of this novel are the solutions to successive Guardian ‘Quick Crosswords’ that appeared through sixty days in 1985 from 3 April to 1 June

You can read more about it at Prospect magazine . Thanks for your responses to last month’s assurance that all of our crosswords are created by human beings, best summarised by Kazoom :

Am glad you’ve posted this. The ‘created by AI’ comments, often supported by zero evidence, have become quite tedious to read. It’s OK to fail, or just not get into the groove on a particular day, but just accept that’s a you problem.

articles.content:
The US manager’s relationship with the international job has changed with a full World Cup cycle beginning

I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff of a literary classic: his imperfect partner who called things off at the first sign of trouble must merely check in on him occasionally to rekindle hopes of a reunion.

Perhaps a bit extreme, but this week’s revelation – that he’d return to Tottenham even if they were relegated and chalking his absence up to imperfect timing, not the part about handing the club a decade-old title – has implicity laid out the terms of his return as United States manager. Others may always have interest in his services, and a certain North London suitor will never get the door slammed in their face outright.

“Now it’s a four-year contract, it’s different,” Pochettino said this week. “We can next season lose the Copa América or the Gold Cup, they’re not happy with us and they can sack us. Or we can say: ‘OK. It’s not in the way that we think.’ Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it’s a different, different type [of thing]. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years to the next World Cup . But now it’s a long period.”

If you’re a Spurs fan, it warms the heart to revisit last decade’s glory days. If you’re a US fan, you’re quite sick of hearing so much about a team besides the one he’s managing. If you’ve been cursed to support both, this must be a very confusing time. And if you’re US Soccer, you know that you no longer have an ace in the hole to outflank any outside interest.

One can’t undersell the appeal of coaching a World Cup host team, with a direct path to Pot One and raucous support for every match. Already a familiar face to Americans who follow the sport, Pochettino became a genuine sensation in the broader sports landscape. Millions of Americans had parallel thoughts that he, clad handsomely in a $500 safari shirt, resembled Russell Crowe – perhaps tacitly revealing that millions of Americans have long undersold the appeal of Russell Crowe.

Compared to his previous post at Chelsea, the US job offered relative reprieve. Never before has Pochettino been such a prolific fixture on hours-long podcasts. The stop/start cadence of international management is appealing for the football men who have grown weary of the meticulous corporatization of the club game. In that sense, Pochettino is among esteemed company.

What’s different about Pochettino from, say, Klopp is his perceived eagerness to return to the club grind. Even atop the Red Bull Football conglomerate, Klopp was quick to brush aside any insinuations about returning to management. Pochettino, by contrast, held talks with Milan about their coaching vacancy immediately before the 2026 World Cup.

There may be a simple answer. Each of Ancelotti, Guardiola, and Klopp – company with which Pochettino is regularly associated – has been the champion of England and Europe. Pochettino, at this stage, has not reached those summits.

Is aiming for a Copa América semi-final more enticing than restoring Tottenham to previous heights? What about reaching a World Cup quarter-final an ocean away from the tens of thousands who soundtracked the previous one? What can US Soccer offer that his caliber of clubs – Tottenham and beyond – can’t exceed?

While Pochettino and his charges have something resembling an excuse for their lack of execution against Belgium, the fact remains that the USMNT were once again eliminated in the last-16. Just like they were under Bob Bradley in 2010. And Jürgen Klinsmann in 2014. And Gregg Berhalter in 2022.

In theory, Pochettino will enter his second cycle in a position of strength having undertaken a thorough examination of the player pool. The fresh faces are no longer MLS journeymen or players in Europe’s lesser divisions. Instead, they’re promising prospects: 16-year-old wonderkid Cavan Sullivan , new Crystal Palace showman Zavier Gozo , highly anticipated La Masia netminder Diego Kochen.

If anything, working the up-and-comers into the established core and identifying sturdier central defenders to partner with Chris Richards should be an incredibly exciting project. The core is in great shape, with this summer’s headliners – Folarin Balogun, Alex Freeman, Richards, and Malik Tillman – all aged 30 or younger in the summer of 2030. There’s plenty of reason to think that the program is better positioned for a deep run at the next World Cup than the 2026.

Actualizing that potential will require a clear vision and a dedicated effort to raise this team’s standard throughout every window of the next four years. Batting eyelashes at past employers hardly projects that level of dedication. And so, for the next four years just like the past one, the biggest question surrounding the USMNT won’t be how far they can go in 2030. It’ll be whether Pochettino will still be the man leading them there.

articles.content:
‘Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry’ will culminate on US soil on Saturday, a staging post on the road to America hosting the World Cup in 2031

W hen New Zealand and South Africa kick off at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore on Saturday, there will be more at stake than victory in “Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry”, the four-Test series the Springboks lead 2-1 . For World Rugby CEO Alan Gilpin, the game is a key staging post on the road to the 2031 World Cup, which the US will host – a journey that could include Six Nations games on American soil .

“We’ve been in a long process with venues and cities, over the last two years,” Gilpin said, of the build to World Cup kick-off. “We’ve still got 25-plus cities involved in that process, which is fantastic in terms of engagement and enthusiasm.

“We’ve now done all the basic feasibility, on, ‘Can we play World Cup-standard rugby in these venues, natural turf,’ all the things we’ve got to take into consideration. Now we’re starting to get submissions from the venue, the city, the state sports commission, on what are some of the commercials, economics, provision of services, city by city, venue by venue. And then you overlay tournament window considerations, availability, NFL, MLS and other considerations, and then weather, team movement.”

In Baltimore, the weather will be hot and sticky, thunderstorms a chance. For the All Blacks and Springboks, team movement meant a shared flight soon after last Saturday’s game in Soweto, won 29-24 by the Boks . The joint journey was unusual but the world is these days. It’s the first weekend of the NFL season. That may seem like commercial suicide for Gilpin but he noted an irony: as World Rugby makes its big play in Baltimore (with the Ravens in Indianapolis to face the Colts), the NFL is in rugby territory, Australia , for San Francisco 49ers v Los Angeles Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. Such is globalization.

“Our ambition is to get to Rugby World Cup in Australia [next year] and be able to say these are the smaller number of venues that will host matches in 2031,” Gilpin said. “There’s a lot of different moving parts. … We had matches this year in a number of small venues, for USA Rugby. There’s some learnings you take from that, but there’s nothing like using the sort of venues that we could use for a World Cup.”

Baltimore seems well set. The field is grass so there’s no need to drop in a pitch, a process at some stadiums used by the soccer World Cup that prompts thoughts of scrums sliding about on pallets but which Gilpin said research showed would work for rugby. Charm City is close to New York, Philadelphia and Washington DC, American rugby towns also full of general sports fans and easily reached from Europe.

On that score, depressingly, World Rugby has had to consider possible problems for fans flying in. Put simply, the present US administration doesn’t like foreigners much. Then again, one group Donald Trump does like is white South Africans, “refugees” admitted in thousands . A thought: show Stephen Miller, Trump’s immigration Nosferatu, how the Springbok pack destroyed the All Blacks in Soweto, and you’ll have rugby content pinged out to Maga faster than ICE can swarm a blue city. Then again, best not tell Trump and his “communist”-hating pals South Africa’s pack is led by a terrifying hooker named Marx .

So much for lefty facetiousness. World Rugby focuses on sport. A sell-out of 71,000 will be a record for rugby in the US. How many fans are from the US game, proudly wearing colors of high school, college or club, will be key to see. The stadium announcer will be Matt McCarthy of RugbyWrapUp , a legend of the game in New York. TV-wise, the game will be “on Paramount Plus with CBS Sports Network doing some highlights,” Gilpin said. “We’ve got to work with them over the next two years on getting all that content in place.”

Next year is a World Cup year. That usually truncates international schedules but Gilpin said big games would be back in America: “There’s going to be a full Rugby Championship played in a Rugby World Cup year for the first time, which is really interesting because we’re a bit later with our start date in Australia, 1 October … so that’s presenting some opportunities for potential conversation. We definitely will have some marquee matches. That’s hopefully some news we’ll be able to share in the not too distant future.” He subsequently shared news with the British press, saying the Six Nations could come into the mix.

“This isn’t a live discussion of an Italy v Ireland game, but why don’t we use that as an example?” Gilpin told the Daily Telegraph . “You’ve got two fantastic fanbases in the US of Irish and Italian fans. If you could take a Six Nations game to the right place, to Boston or to New York … you can definitely drive the economics. Now, you’re going to have Irish fans and Italian fans in those respective home countries saying, ‘Hang on a minute, you know, we want to see our country play?’ The counter-argument to that [is] it’s still Irish and Italian fans getting the chance to watch their team, so they’re just not the ones who live in Ireland and Italy on this occasion. But that’s a balancing piece we’ve got to work through.”

Speaking to the Guardian, Gilpin promised “learnings” from the last big US game featuring Ireland, the All Blacks’ win at Soldier Field in Chicago last November which featured technical snafus around a dubious red card .

“We’re more directly involved with the two unions and with the match promoter in the way sports presentation looks,” Gilpin said. “How do you make sure the audience is engaged in the right way with big screens and match-day activity? So we’re dialing that up. It’s a learning curve the whole time.”

In terms of what there is to be learned about the state of the American game, Gilpin like many is concerned about Major League Rugby, the US men’s league now down to just five teams . Latest to leave was Anthem Rugby Carolina, which World Rugby and USA Rugby funded for three years to grow domestic talent. The governing body trumpets a $200m investment for 2031 and the women’s World Cup two years later. Money spent on bringing in the All Blacks and Springboks is part of that total but so is grassroots work.

“In all the work we’re doing with USA Rugby, there’s obviously the community and college and club and youth and high school pieces,” Gilpin said. “But on the high-performance national programs … look at the last six months.” Both Eagles sevens teams are doing well and the men’s 15s have won four games on the trot , three in the Nations Cup, a World Rugby event. On Saturday in Osaka, in the Pacific Nations Cup, the Eagles face Japan .

About the demise of Anthem, Gilpin stayed off record. Sources say a potential sixth team is in the MLR mix but there isn’t much likelihood of the Anthem experiment being repeated, even in light of successful sub-national World Rugby projects such as the Fijian Drua. Of MLR, Gilpin said there were “continuous conversations. There’s no doubt that the improving performance of the Eagles must be helpful to those conversations.”

Back to Baltimore. The first three All Blacks-Springboks Tests were brutal thrillers. Now the All Blacks, without injured men like great No 8 Ardie Savea, must find salvation. In the city of Stringer Bell, Jimmy McNulty and other hard-boiled heroes , World Rugby will hope for a finale that goes down to the wire.

Martin Pengelly writes on rugby in the US on Substack, at The National Maul .

articles.summary: Make the most of the early-autumn glut of fruit with this quick, squidgy-crumbed bake that’s bursting with berries Every year, I get annoyed with myself for not making the most of blackberry season, and then it’s gone before I’ve had a chance really to enjoy them. articles.content:
Make the most of the early-autumn glut of fruit with this quick, squidgy-crumbed bake that’s bursting with berries

E very year, I get annoyed with myself for not making the most of blackberry season, and then it’s gone before I’ve had a chance really to enjoy them. They’re such great berries to bake with, and here I’ve scattered them in a simple ricotta cake. It’s a quick, one-bowl bake with a perfectly squidgy crumb that’s bursting with fruit.

170g caster sugar Finely grated zest of 2 unwaxed lemons 2 large eggs 70g olive oil 125g ricotta 130g plain flour 1 tsp baking powder ¼ tsp salt 150g blackberries

To finish 125g ricotta 1 tbsp lemon juice ½ tbsp icing sugar , plus extra for dusting

Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line a 23cm loose-bottomed cake tin.

Put the sugar and lemon zest in a bowl and use your fingertips to rub together until fragrant. Add the eggs and oil, whisk until frothy, then mix in the ricotta. Finally, sift in the flour, baking powder and salt, and stir gently to combine.

Pour the batter into the lined tin, scatter the blackberries on top, and bake for 28-32 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the middle comes out clean. Leave the cake to cool completely in its tin, then turn out and dust with icing sugar.

For the whipped ricotta, whisk all the ingredients in a bowl until smooth and creamy; alternatively, for a super-smooth result, blitz it in a food processor.

articles.content:
Some people don’t understand my lifelong enthusiasm for roadside stop-offs – now visiting and cataloguing them is what I do for a living

W hen I was 10 years old, the highlight of my summer holidays was going to work with my dad, who is a lorry driver. For a couple of years in the mid-2000s, I’d excitedly climb into the cab next to him and we’d set off on a 10-hour trip. My job was to follow the AA Road Atlas, and I’d joyfully track the services marked on the map as we thundered along.

My dad thought stopping was a waste of time, but his designated rest stops were my favourite part of the trip. Depending on the journey, we might stop for two or three meals. I always hoped at least one would be at a Little Chef. I loved their Olympic Breakfast, a massive full English, and every meal was rounded off with a lollipop – what more could a 10-year-old want?

As I got older, motorway services retained their air of magic. In 2012, when I was 14, I found the website motorwayservices.uk , which reviewed lots of major service stations. Any time my family visited one, I’d take pictures and contribute to the site.

I learned to drive as soon as I turned 17 and bought myself a two-door Smart car, which I still drive today. After I passed my test, I’d drive out to services near my home in Bristol.

After leaving school, I got a job as a bus driver, but I soon realised that, while I loved the driving, there wasn’t enough time for stopping. I carried on visiting as many services as I could on my days off, just as a hobby, but soon I decided to try to make this my job.

I left the bus company and started posting more reviews to the site and my own social media channels under the name The Services King . Now it’s my full-time job. Alongside reviews, I write articles for industry publications and do sponsored posts on social media.

I love the history connected to service stations, how they chart the growth of Britain’s road network and our changing tastes in food. In my view, the services are the destination, not just part of the journey. There’s an underlying sense of occasion connected to them.

I hit the milestone of visiting every one of the UK’s 97 motorway service stations in 2019. I revisit them all periodically to review and post updates on their facilities, as well as visiting smaller rest stops on A roads. I work away from home four days a week and can visit up to five service stations a day, although I don’t always stop for something to eat and drink. I see what’s new since my last visit and photograph the facilities so drivers can plan their stops.

I like to include a bit of history or trivia about each service station. My most popular posts are usually new site openings, and my followers come from all walks of life, but lots are industry professionals.

My dad struggles to understand my obsession. Sometimes people don’t believe me when I tell them what I do for a living, but it’s always a conversation starter. Everyone has something to say about services. I think of them as one of life’s great levellers; no matter who you are, or where you’re from, everybody has the shared experience of visiting one.

There are a few key factors that make an exemplary service station; bonus points if it has a notable landmark and looks unusual – for instance, the Pennine Tower at Lancaster services on the M6, or a bridge where you can sit and have a coffee watching the cars go by underneath you. Some stations now have lovely outdoor features; Rugby services has gardens and a fountain. Most people prefer it if they’re easy to get to – straight off the motorway is better than having to come off at a junction and navigate roundabouts.

I’m always asked what my favourite station is. I don’t have one, but I do favour those that have a proper sit-down area to eat a meal and relax. As so many of them are full of chains these days, independently owned Tebay, on the M6, and Gloucester, on the M5, which have farm shops and a proper restaurant, are high on my list.

I really enjoy my job, but it’s a lot of travel. I can easily cover 25,000 miles in a year. When I take time off, I like to holiday in the UK, so wherever I go, I can’t escape the services. Not that I’d want to. To me, they will always be the best part of any holiday.

articles.content:
The coffee and cream pudding has always been popular. But now it’s inspired a dedicated cafe and countless products, from drinks to ice-creams to buns. What’s behind this big cultural craving?

W hen Giancarlo Fanigliulo opened Marrone, a cafe dedicated to tiramisu in London’s Soho in August, he hadn’t anticipated he would sell out within two and a half hours. “I was expecting a buzz, but I wasn’t expecting queues around the corner,” he tells me. “It was insane.”

This kind of excitement about the Italian dessert is not a one-off – we are, it seems, living in an age of tiramisu-mania. Nearly all of the high street coffee chains have offered some kind of tiramisu coffee as a seasonal special (in the US, Dunkin’ currently has four different tiramisu-flavoured drinks on its menu). Meanwhile, Haagen-Dazs and Carte D’or now sell tiramisu ice-cream, London chain Buns from Home offers a tiramisu-flavoured croissant-dough bun and social media is awash with tiramisu recipes and videos of “tiramisu drawers” – trays of the dessert ready to serve out of drawers in chefs’ kitchens – as popularised by the viral one at Manchester pasta restaurant Onda.

Marrone is not the first “just tiramisu” vendor to pop up in recent years: Sheffield’s Paradiso – which, along with classic tiramisu, will sell you a “latte-misù” (an iced coffee topped with a slab of tiramisu) – opened in 2023; while the TikTok viral Secret Layers , where you can buy the dessert from a tiny hatch in a wall, opened in Paddington, London, last year. In March, the Guinness World Record for the world’s longest tiramisu was broken when chefs assembled a 440.6 metre portion of the pudding (although there was some discussion, among my friends at least, about whether it should actually count as the longest, since it appeared to be a series of smaller portions of tiramisu joined together).

Supermarkets are also noticing an uptick in tiramisu purchases. “Sales of our own brand tiramisu range have grown by 5% over the last year, with our Tesco Finest Coffee & Amaretto Tiramisu Dessert , proving particularly popular, selling nearly 10% more,” says Peter Wood, Tesco’s category buying manager for desserts. M&S, which is currently stocking “creamy tiramisu brownies” and, at Easter, sold tiramisu hot cross buns, says tiramisu sales are up 27% compared with last year.

The tiramisu trend has reached weddings, too, sometimes as a replacement for a wedding cake. The dessert “is probably one of the main trends of 2026,” says Cotswolds-based wedding planner Oliver Stanton – when we speak, he has just finished working on a wedding where tiramisu featured. “A lot of couples are having tiramisu served in coupe glasses and arranged in a tower like you would with a champagne tower. It serves as an extra photo opportunity as well as dessert for the guests.”

Tiramisu has always been a beloved pudding, but Lisa Harris, co-founder of Harris and Hayes food and drink consultancy , can see why it is enjoying a spike in popularity at the moment: social media algorithms reward nostalgia and anything that symbolises decadence – and tiramisu does both: “A good tiramisu is actually an exercise of this balance of the coffee, the cream and the sponge. There’s sort of not that much to it,” says Harris. “And yet it’s also this shorthand for indulgence.”

The emergence of “Little Treat Culture” – the concept of giving yourself small rewards amid trying political and economic times – has also aided the success of tiramisu and tiramisu-flavoured products. At a time “when people are perhaps eating out less, in the current economic climate,” indulgence becomes more coveted. Someone “just thinking about what dessert they’re going to have” is a bigger deal, Harris says.

It was partly because tiramisu has become “such a culture” that Fanigliulo decided to open Marrone. The 30-year-old doesn’t have a background in hospitality – he previously worked in tech sales – but he was struck that “when you think of tiramisu, there’s never been a brand associated with it”. His family is Italian on his father’s side, and his tiramisu is inspired by his grandmother’s recipe. All three of the tiramisus on Marrone’s menu (original classic, dark chocolate and sea salt, and pistachio, each sold for £10 a pot) are light and glossy in style – as opposed to a block that retains its shape when cut into – which is how Fanigliulo prefers his tiramisu. He is hoping that Marrone will become a go-to spot for people after this style of tiramisu (which, I can confirm, is absolutely delicious).

Fanigliulo’s enthusiasm for good tiramisu is infectious, and reminds me that I do actually really love this beautiful, creamy, caffeine-and-booze-filled pudding. And I’m all for there being more places to get great tiramisu. But whenever I see a new modification of this beautiful dessert into yet another drink or snack, I can’t help but think we might be overdoing it a little. Perhaps it’s time to make it tirami-stop?

articles.content:
One set may have already passed in her first US Open semi-final, but Elena Rybakina still had not arrived inside Arthur Ashe Stadium. While an inspired Coco Gauff blew through the first stanza covering every inch of the acrylic surface as their 22,000-strong audience screamed for the Kazakhstani’s blood, Rybakina was wild and erratic from the baseline and her peerless serve was nowhere to be seen.

Nobody reaches the summit of professional without being able to problem-solve through difficult days on court though, and Rybakina gave a brilliant showcase of the underrated toughness at the heart of her success as she coolly recovered from a set down to overpower Gauff and seal her spot in her first US Open final with a 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 win.

Six matches into her latest grand slam odyssey, Rybakina has not played her best tennis at any point in the tournament but her continued success here underlines her mental growth. This is Rybakina’s fourth career grand slam final and since her maiden victory at Wimbledon in 2022, her subsequent three major finals have all come on hard courts. Having waited four years to win her second grand slam, she has given herself a shot at winning two major titles in the same year.

In many ways, this was already one of the most important and successful tournaments of Rybakina’s career. She arrived in New York with a golden opportunity to unlock one of the great achievements in this sport by becoming world No 1. Despite a scary Achilles injury in the build up to the tournament and a dire record at the US Open, she kept on moving forward.

In the aftermath of that massive success, which she sealed with a tense quarter-final win over Zheng Qinwen, Rybakina made it clear that she was far from satisfied and the job was not even half-finished. She was here for nothing less than the title. Now she will contend for it in a final that will mark the rekindling of the rivalry that has defined the season, facing the departing No 1 Aryna Sabalenka in a rematch of the Australian Open final won by Rybakina.

articles.content:
The brilliantly strange experimental band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flair

T heir masks light up now. To the extent there was a hard news event from Wednesday’s exhilarating sold-out New York debut of Angine de Poitrine , that was it. The Québécois duo went viral in corners of the internet earlier this year thanks in part to their microtonal, odd-metered take on hard-driving rock, but also because of those ostentatious costumes and masks – black and white polka dot tunics and jumpsuits with oversized papier-mache faces and exaggerated features, originally featuring golden glittery eyes and signature pyramid accoutrements. The new ones have all those same things but with the added ability to light up in a bright yellow at key moments.

A small detail, to be sure, but one got the sense that the weeknight crowd was reveling in it and many others at New York’s Le Poisson Rouge (LPR) – an appropriately French-named venue given the band’s home province. Wednesday was the first of the band’s two shows at the 700-capacity basement venue renowned for its sound system and commitment to adventurous programming. Both Angine shows had been sold out for many months, ever since a video of them playing in a French studio was uploaded to KEXP’s YouTube channel and went viral. At time of writing, the video is closing in on 20m views – a remarkable tally given that the music, by mass-appeal standards, is so magnificently odd.

While their success came suddenly, Angine de Poitrine had spent years perfecting ways of expanding small details into fully formed musical themes, using them to bring new life to the repetitious riffs that form an ever-evolving backbone of each of their lengthy songs. Added to the outfits, the masks, the double-necked guitar/bass, even their consonant-heavy song titles and stage names (Klek, drummer, and Khn, guitarist/bassist) and commitment to near-total anonymity, they have created an intoxicating mystery. Listeners are left free to wonder what this mysterious duo are playing, why it sticks in the mind like a pop song despite its timings and tunings, and how the hell they are physically able to play it with all that stuff on them.

Seeing them live might have answered some of those questions, but it also raised others. The band’s signature sound is defined by dearth of reverb and sustain – would deadened drums and defined guitar play in a noisy concert hall? Their signature image is that of aliens who have beamed into a studio with no rough edges. Would that play once you can see the cables emerging from out the back of their costumes? With such little difference between the album and in-studio live versions of their songs, and their expert use of live looping creating few opportunities to vamp, would the live concert even be worthwhile?

Yes, it absolutely would. The band emerged in full regalia to a roar, packed in under LPR’s low-slung ceiling. They blasted their way through Angor, the closer from Vol II, the second of their two albums, then raised the bar with Yor Zarad, another of that album’s ferocious highlights. Tamebsz, from the 2024 release Vol I followed, for the first time making use of the light-up masks to guide the audience in an especially complicated game of call-and-response. The songs had not especially changed from how they sound on their albums and in-studios. The ability to finally see the duo’s superb musicianship up close carried the show – as did the reminders that they are still human. How does a musician performing in a giant mask take a drink of water? Through special water bottles with comically long, glow-in-the-dark rubber straws.

Three-quarters through, though, the perils of live performance intruded. Khn had broken a string. And when you break a string on a specially built two-necked guitar/bass with custom microtonal frettings to access notes between the western scale, well, it’s not like you can borrow somebody else’s. And given their costumes, it’s also not like you can change the string yourself without difficulty. Khn required the help of a guitar tech to guide a replacement string through the back of the instrument, all while Khn himself partook in an impromptu jam with Klek using the other strings on the instrument. When that string change didn’t take, the duo figured they had delayed long enough and launched into Sarniezz – by necessity, the only time some of those signature riffs rendered a bit differently.

And when they unplugged and left the stage, no encore followed, and none was demanded. Questions had either been answered, or pleasantly remained.

articles.title: ‘I’ve got more of a sense of humour than Ralph Lauren’ – nine things we learned from Paul Smith’s new memoir
articles.summary: He put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripes In July, the British designer Paul Smith celebrated his 80th birthday and he has now released a memoir to mark the occasion. Threads: My Life in Style tells Smith’s story, from growing up in Nottingham and leaving school with no qualifications to selling suits to celebs, including Gary Oldman and David Bowie. Here are nine of our favourite lesser-known takeaways from the book. Continue reading...
articles.content:
He put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripes

I n July, the British designer Paul Smith celebrated his 80th birthday and he has now released a memoir to mark the occasion. Threads: My Life in Style tells Smith’s story, from growing up in Nottingham and leaving school with no qualifications to selling suits to celebs, including Gary Oldman and David Bowie.

1. He made boxers something you want to be seen in In the 70s, Smith reimagined boxers in clashing prints and colours, such as polka dots and stripes rather than drab greys and whites, catapulting them from the back of the underwear drawer to the pages of fashion magazines. “I always describe my early success as nudging rather than shoving the British male into appreciating the fact that you could be a little different,” he writes.

2. He has a love/hate relationship with stripes Smith describes the multi-stripe he has become synonymous with as “both a joy and a curse”. It was a design detail forced upon him in his early days due to budget constraints, but quickly became popular among his customers. “It began to take on a life of its own,” Smith writes. However, it “became a bit of a burden to me if to no one else. You meet people who say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who’s famous for the stripes.’ It’s like being Calvin Klein – you can make beautiful clothes every year but someone will always say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who makes underpants.’ You find yourself having to work around it.”

In the 1980s, Smith says men only bought two types of socks: plain or argyle patterned. After coming across a pair with a paperclip motif in Japan, he brought the design to the UK. Now he sells more than 700,000 pairs of socks a year. “Quite often when I’m introduced to someone new he’ll say, ‘Oh yes – I get your socks for Christmas,’” Smith writes.

4. His office is the original example of curated chaos Piles of vinyl records, 28 bicycles (including the yellow Pinarello Chris Froome rode to victory in the Tour de France), a model train set, hundreds of books and oil paintings and a Snoopy telephone are just some of the curiosities you’ll find in Smith’s office. And then there are the rabbit figurines in all shapes and sizes, the result of a joke, which got out of hand, about how they were his lucky charm. “Every week I get rabbits of all kinds,” writes Smith. “They’re everywhere. Rabbits made of bronze, felt, plastic, wood, stone. A man in Italy sends me four or five a month, even though I’ve never met him.”

Bowie became a big fan of Smith’s two-piece suits, including one in a lemon and pink overcheck. After turning up to the store unannounced several times to shop, Smith invited him for a cup of tea in his studio. It was the beginning of a friendship. Bowie never called Smith by his first name – instead, it was always Smithy. “Was he an easy person to be with and to talk to? Only if you were interesting,” writes Smith. “There was no small talk.”

Even if you’ve never been to LA, you’ll probably recognise Smith’s Melrose Avenue store. Five years after it opened in 2005, Instagram launched and the store’s hot-pink wall became a selfie sensation. There have been thousands of snaps taken at the #pinkwall, making it one of the most Instagrammed buildings in California.

7. He’s not keen on comparisons to Ralph Lauren Smith describes getting “pissed off” in his early days when the press kept comparing him to the American designer, and renowned anglophile, Ralph Lauren. “I’ve got far more of a sense of humour, for a start,” he writes. “His shops were always so serious, with the stately-home image and the good-looking models. There was nobody that English in England.”

As a huge cycling enthusiast (he hoped to become a pro until he had a nasty accident aged 17), Smith was thrilled to be asked to design the leaders’ jerseys for the annual Giro d’Italia bike race in 201. It included the “maglia rosa”, a pink jersey that is (sort of) equivalent to the Tour de France’s yellow jersey. Smith added some red piping around the edge, signature striping on the left sleeve and a tiny sketch of a cyclist. It was sent to Pope Francis to be blessed. Smith writes: “I’ve done a lot of collaborations over the years, from cars to crayons, from carpets to cycles, but only one of them, so far as I’m aware, has been personally blessed by the pope.”

9. Despite all his success, he remains a do er Case in point, during lockdown Smith continued to work from his office, albeit alone. One day he was met by an unpleasant smell and discovered that 18 containers of forgotten milk had exploded all over the kitchen floor. He spent three hours cleaning it up. At one stage he found himself thinking: “I wonder if my friend Giorgio Armani is doing something like this now?” Still, when Smith told colleagues about his wiping marathon, “they all said the same thing: ‘Oh no! Only Paul Smith.’ And I took that as a compliment.”

articles.content:
Tony Benn v Ali G | Ancient knitting | Picky bits | More nominative determinism

Sacha Baron Cohen may have tricked Tony Benn into thinking that Ali G was a real person, but he certainly didn’t succeed in making a fool of him ( Booyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern Britain, 5 September ). Matching the robustness of his answers to that of Ali G’s questions, Benn displayed no condescension or snobbery. Instead his response was a masterclass in courtesy, based on the view that anyone is entitled to ask questions, however far removed their speech is from that of an Oxford don. The laugh was rather on Baron Cohen. Vivien Bailey St Albans

I beg to differ with Richard Ross ( Letters, 9 September ) about the invasion of England by William of Orange. He was invited to this country by politicians who wanted to remove the Catholic James II. The only reason William came with troops was to defeat the resistance of James’s loyal followers. Shirley Pritchard Wimbledon, London

My late wife, Pat Green, always maintained that the elaborate hairstyle of the Willendorf Venus ( Olga Soffer obituary, 16 August ) was in fact knitted; not only that, but it was the blackberry stitch used by her, passed down through the generations via her mother. Richard Dowsett Potton, Bedfordshire

Picky bits? Party tea ( Letters, 3 September )? This sounds like a buffet, or as our family called it, a “grab, sit and gobble”. Richard Crosher Sheffield

I would have liked to succeed in the nominative determinism game ( Letters, 9 September ), but too few people know a rare bookbinding term . I folded. Michael Quinion Thornbury, Gloucestershire

These letters are doing my head in. I think I’ll go and sit quietly to engrave a small piece of whale ivory. Lynne Scrimshaw London

I shouldn’t contribute to this topic – as I will only spoil it for everyone. Alexander Marr Gosport, Hampshire

articles.title: A scientist said bananas ‘kill’ the benefit of blueberries. Is that true?
articles.summary: Can blending these popular fruits in a smoothie adversely affect the berries’ nutritional benefits? Experts weigh in This year was shaping up to be a banner year for bananas: they were lauded as “ 2026’s big viral taste ”, landed pride of place as Prada’s new lip balm flavor, and were even deemed “ the next pumpkin spice ”. But this summer, the Mel Robbins Podcast featured Dr Rhonda Patrick, a biomedical scientist, who said that adding banana to a blueberry smoothie could adversely affect the nutritional benefits of the berries. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Can blending these popular fruits in a smoothie adversely affect the berries’ nutritional benefits? Experts weigh in

T his year was shaping up to be a banner year for bananas: they were lauded as “ 2026’s big viral taste ”, landed pride of place as Prada’s new lip balm flavor, and were even deemed “ the next pumpkin spice ”.

But this summer, the Mel Robbins Podcast featured Dr Rhonda Patrick, a biomedical scientist, who said that adding banana to a blueberry smoothie could adversely affect the nutritional benefits of the berries.

Could the beloved mashup of blueberries and bananas really be a bad match?

Patrick’s claim involved an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase, which appears in bananas, and polyphenols, an umbrella term for a diverse family of antioxidant compounds found in plants – including blueberries.

“Polyphenol oxidase, it’s essentially an enzyme that’s breaking down the polyphenols. And there have now been studies … showing if you add bananas to blueberries, you’re not getting as many polyphenols. In fact, it’s quite a bit lower. So the banana is killing the benefit,” she said .

The most likely source for Patrick’s claim is a 2023 study that explored how polyphenol oxidase affected the body’s absorption of particular polyphenols called flavanols.

The study found that participants who drank banana smoothies with added flavanol had lower blood levels of these antioxidants than those who drank mixed-berry smoothies with the same additive.

There are a few reasons not to rely too heavily on this study for this specific claim.

First of all, the researchers “never, ever made a smoothie with bananas and blueberries together”, says Dr Joe Schwarcz, a science communicator and director of McGill University’s office for science and society.

Further, the study “only had eight subjects … not a big enough number to have significant conclusions”, says Schwarcz.

But zooming out to the effects of polyphenol oxidase on flavanols, “there is a statistical difference in the amount of polyphenols that may be present in your smoothie as the result of the banana,” says Schwarcz.

I reached out to Patrick at her health content company, FoundMyFitness, to clarify her claim. A spokesperson, Dan (their full name was not provided on request), responded by email: “The fact that this enzyme breaks down some polyphenols is essentially beyond reproach and not dependent on any one study she cites.”

A body of research does support that polyphenol oxidase influences the antioxidative capacity of different compounds in fruit and vegetables in various different ways .

But context is important. Blueberries contain several types of polyphenols. Anthocyanins, which are responsible for the color of blueberries, are proportionally more significant and abundant in the fruit than flavanols, says Schwarcz.

Anthocyanins are associated with a range of potential health benefits, including reduced risk of overall mortality, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

Thus, what this study measured was “not even the important compounds of blueberries”, says Schwarcz.

Finally, this study was funded by the Mars company – and the flavanols used in this project were derived from cocoa.

“And it just so happens that [Mars] sells flavanol supplements” and chocolate, which contains flavanols, says Schwarcz.

“Some nutrients enhance the absorption of other nutrients, like vitamin C and iron. Others can reduce absorption, such as the oxalates in spinach, which bind to calcium and reduce its bioavailability.”

But in the grand scheme of your diet, Northrop says you shouldn’t lose sleep over such interactions.

“Rather than trying to micromanage every food combination, I encourage people to focus on the bigger picture: eat a varied diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, seeds and other nutrient-dense foods to meet your body’s needs,” she says.

Eating too few fruits and vegetables is a bigger concern than optimizing polyphenol absorption from every smoothie, says Northrop.

“Most of us aren’t consuming the recommended five servings of fruits and vegetables daily. If adding a banana makes a berry smoothie more delicious and encourages someone to eat more fruit, I see that as a win,” she says.

Polyphenol-rich foods have been associated with a range of potential health benefits, including supporting cardiovascular and metabolic health, promoting a healthy gut microbiome, and helping prevent chronic diseases, says Northrop.

Evidence suggests that consuming between 400 and 600mg of flavanols daily from foods such as green tea, cocoa and apples may support cardiometabolic health, including potential improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar regulation.

But unlike with vitamin and mineral deficiencies, which can cause distinct negative health effects, “we don’t know the physiological effects of polyphenol insufficiency on health. Polyphenols are not considered essential nutrients, and there isn’t an established recommended daily intake for total polyphenols,” Northrop says.

If you’re really worried about your berry smoothie’s flavanol levels, add fruit that is lower in polyphenol oxidase than banana, such as mango or pineapple.

Or, experiment with different ingredients. “Oats, yogurt, silken tofu, kefir, avocado and frozen cauliflower are popular smoothie add-ins that can offer a similar creamy thickness as a banana,” Gaw adds.

“In the context of your overall diet,” the interplay of bananas and berries is “insignificant”, says Schwarcz. Overall, it’s good to eat a variety of fruits, and we benefit from their varied antioxidant compounds.

Schwarcz has seen the idea of focusing on a specific food component and its impact on human health bubble up in nutrition literature for years.

“Your health is a very complex business of nutrition, of genetics, of your activity levels. And to try to make a big deal out of whether you put a banana in your smoothie or not – it’s just scientific nonsense,” he says. “It makes no practical difference in your life.”

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel on RNC convention: ‘They’re very nervous about the midterms, and rightly so’
articles.summary: Late-night hosts recapped the Republican event in Dallas and calls to ban Zohran Mamdani from 9/11 ceremonies Late-night hosts roasted the Republican National Committee’s underattended “midterm convention” and attempts to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, from 9/11 remembrances. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Late-night hosts recapped the Republican event in Dallas and calls to ban Zohran Mamdani from 9/11 ceremonies

Late-night hosts roasted the Republican National Committee’s underattended “midterm convention” and attempts to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, from 9/11 remembrances.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with the news that financial disclosures revealed how Donald Trump gave his aide and “least secret admirer” Natalie Harp a $45,000 cash gift for the holidays last December. Harp “is the woman who praises him, shows him his iPad, keeps him distracted, and in return he gave her a wad of cash – like you do a babysitter, like you do when a neighbor girl comes over and does a diaper change,” Kimmel quipped.

Trump also gave similarly sized cash gifts to two other young female staffers. “But I just want to say, before you rush to any judgment, there’s absolutely nothing unusual about an 80-year-old billionaire president giving the three young attractive women in his office 45,000 bucks each,” said Kimmel. “ You’re the weird one for even thinking that, and shame on you.”

Kimmel then turned to the Republican National Committee’s unusual “midterm convention” , a two-day affair in Dallas aimed at convincing Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has led the US into an increasingly unpopular war .

“They never had a midterm convention before, but Trump wanted one and so they’re having it,” Kimmel explained. “The president, he’s hyping this . He’s saying it’s ‘the greatest rally of them all’. He said it’s ‘really hot’, it’s ‘totally sold out’, which is funny because the RNC had to hand out a bunch of free tickets to this sold-out event.”

A large number of Republican lawmakers have also opted out of the convention due to “scheduling conflicts” and “not wanting to be anywhere near him right now”, Kimmel noted. “They’re very nervous about the midterms and rightly so. They are in serious danger of losing bigly.”

They’re in danger, in fact, of losing a Senate seat in Texas to the Democratic candidate James Talarico, whom Kimmel will interview on YouTube this week “under unusual circumstances” after a Trump-appointed federal regulator “threatened” his show.

On the Daily Show, Michael Kosta also checked in on the RNC’s rare “midterm convention”. “Everyone is going to be there,” he said before several clips of Republican lawmakers claiming they would in fact not be in attendance, for excuses up to an including a Wednesday night high school football game, “stuff” that was already planned and a “can’t miss dove-hunting event”.

“Yeah, you can’t miss dove hunting!” Kosta quipped. “Eat lead, symbol of peace!”

In other tough news for Republicans, JD Vance told a crowd this week that the country was about to “celebrate” 25 years since the terrorist attacks on 9/11. “Well, we’re not going to celebrate it, JD,” said Kosta. “‘Happy 9/11, everyone! I brought Rice Krispy towers!’

“We’re not going to celebrate 9/11, but we are going to commemorate 9/11,” he continued, “and one thing I always think about is how in the days after the attacks, President Bush made a genuine effort to defend Islam.”

Kosta played a clip from 2001 in which Bush reminded: “These acts of violence against innocents violate the fundamental tenets of the Islamic faith, and it’s important for my fellow Americans to understand that. Islam is peace.”

“Boy, we really didn’t understand how good we had it, did we?” Kosta added. “I mean, I’m not saying this man was perfect, but that was a full, coherent, non-racist sentence. Hindsight, huh?

“The point is, back in 2001, President Bush was imploring the country not to lump all Muslims in with the terrorists who committed 9/11. Now it’s 25 years later so, how’s that going?”

Kosta then cut to a news clips about a petition to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, a Muslim, from the city’s 9/11 ceremony, while Sean Hannity and Fox News’s Laura Ingraham criticized his signing of a proclamation declaring 11 September a city-wide day of remembrance.

“Look, I know nothing I say is going to convince the Mamdani haters, but if you ask me, the idea that 9/11 is about Muslims v America isn’t just wrong, it’s accepting Osama bin Laden’s vision of the world,” Kosta concluded. “And the fact that 25 years after 9/11, we have a New York-grown, Muslim mayor leading our remembrance proves to the world that al-Qaida didn’t win. New York won.

“So yes, everyone is welcome at the New York ceremony, and I would be there … but I’m going dove-hunting and it’s can’t-miss.”

articles.title: The Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughter
articles.summary: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack Five short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity. Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attack

F ive short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity.

Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.”

The best of the stories, In the South , is narrated by Neil Shah who gives characterful voice to two elderly neighbours in Chennai, India, who spend their days bickering with each other on their porches. They are known as Senior and Junior because one is 17 days older than the other. Despite their cantankerousness, the two draw comfort from one another’s presence. When Junior dies on the street after being toppled by a passing Vespa – on the same day that a tsunami hits the south of the country – Senior comes to understand how “death and life [are] just adjacent verandas”.

Kin Tayari Jones , Oneworld Audio , 13 hr, 10 min Angel Pean and Ashley J Hobbs narrate this sweeping tale of two best friends, born a few days apart in Louisiana, who grow up without mothers. As they get older, fate pulls them apart and they pursue different futures.

Land Maggie O’Farrell , Tinder Press, 16 hr 47 mins Not long after the Irish famine, a cartographer’s son must finish a map of Ireland begun by his father away from the prying eyes of the British. This historical novel by the Hamnet author is read by Dane Whyte O’Hara.
